   432	
   433	
   434	\paragraph{Partitioning the registers, and symmetries}
   435	In the remainder of this section as well as \Cref{sec:combining,sec:apply-ldt}, we will partition the six registers
   436	$\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''$ into
   437	two ``parties'' in two different ways. The first is to consider
   438	$\alice \alice'$ together to form  a single party, and $\bob \alice''$
   439	to form the second party. The second is to consider $\bob \bob'$ to
   440	form the first party, and $\alice \bob''$ to form the second
   441	party. Thanks to the symmetry of the Pauli basis test under exchanging the
   442	two players, as well as the symmetry of the ancilla states in
   443	registers $\alice' \alice''$ and $\bob' \bob''$, every ``bipartite'' consistency relation we derive between two
   444	operators $M, N$ will hold for both of the two bipartitioning schemes,
   445	and with the first and second party interchanged. That is, whenever we
   446	derive a bipartite relation of the form
   447	\[ M_{\alice \alice'} \approx_\delta N_{\bob \alice''}, \]
   448	the same steps, with the registers appropriately changed, will also
   449	yield
   450	\begin{align*}
   451	  N_{\alice \alice'} &\approx_{\delta} M_{\bob \alice''}, \\
   452	  M_{\bob \bob'} &\approx_{\delta} N_{\alice \bob''}, \\
   453	  N_{\bob \bob'} &\approx_{\delta} M_{\alice \bob''}.
   454	\end{align*}
   455	
   456	Similarly, whenever we derive a single-party relation of the form
   457	$M_{\alice \alice'} \approx N_{\alice \alice'}$, the same steps with
   458	the registers appropriately changed will also yield the same relation
   459	on $\bob\alice''$, $\bob \bob'$ and $\alice \bob''$. We refer to these
   460	relations as \emph{symmetric equivalents}.
   461	
   462	\begin{lemma}
   463	\label{lem:qld-comm-cons}
   464		There exists a function $\delta_{\acom}(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   465	
   466	
   467	\begin{enumerate}
   468		\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over $r \in \F_q$ and $u\in \F_q^m$, we have 
   469		\[
   470			(\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_a)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_\eps (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_a)_{\bob \alice''}\,.
   471			\]
   472		\item (\textbf{Approximate commutation}) On average over
   473	          uniformly random $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$,
   474	          we have 
   475		\[
   476			(\hat{M}^{(\Point,\xpt),u_\xpt,r_\xpt}_{b}
   477	                \hat{M}^{(\Point,\zpt),u_\zpt,r_\zpt}_{b'})_{\alice
   478	                  \alice'} \approx_{\delta_{\acom}}
   479	                (\hat{M}^{(\Point,\zpt),u_\zpt,r_\zpt}_{b'}
   480	                \hat{M}^{(\Point,\xpt),u_\xpt,r_\xpt}_{b})_{\alice
   481	                  \alice'} \;.
   482		\]
   483	      \end{enumerate}
   484	      Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   485	      also hold.
   486	\end{lemma}
   487	
   488	\begin{proof}
   489	Item 1, the self-consistency of $\{\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_a \}$, follows from the fact that the original points measurements $\{ M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \}$ are approximately self-consistent between registers $\alice$ and $\bob$ in $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ (item~\ref{enu:qld-cons} in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications}), the Pauli projections $\{\tau^W_a(\ind_m(u))\}$ are perfectly self-consistent between registers $\alice'$ and $\alice''$, and~\Cref{fact:data-processing}. 
   490		
   491		We now establish the approximate commutation relations. On average over uniformly random $\omega = (u_\xpt,u_\zpt,r_\xpt,r_\zpt)$, we have
   492		\begin{align*}
   493		&\hat{M}^{(\Point,\xpt),u_\xpt,r_\xpt}_{b} \hat{M}^{(\Point,\zpt),u_\zpt,r_\zpt}_{b'}  \label{eq:qld-m-x-m-z} \\
   494		&= \frac{1}{4} \Big ( \Id + (-1)^b \hat{X}^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt) \Big ) \Big ( \Id + (-1)^{b'} \hat{Z}^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt) \Big ) \\
   495		&= \frac{1}{4} \Big ( \Id + (-1)^b \hat{X}^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt) + (-1)^{b'} \hat{Z}^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt) + (-1)^{b + b'} \hat{X}^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt) \hat{Z}^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt) \Big)\;,
   496		\end{align*}
   497		where the first equality follows from~\eqref{eq:lc-22}.	
   498		Note that
   499		\begin{align*}
   500		\hat{X}^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt)
   501	         & \hat{Z}^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt) \\
   502					&=
   503	                                             X^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt)
   504	                                             Z^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt)
   505	                                             \otimes \tau^X(r_\xpt
   506	                                             \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt))
   507	                                             \tau^Z(r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt)) \\
   508		&\approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} Z^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt)
   509	   X^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt)  \otimes \tau^Z(r_\zpt\cdot \ind_m( u_\zpt))
   510	   \tau^X(r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt)) \\
   511		&= \hat{Z}^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt) \hat{X}^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt)\;, 
   512		\end{align*}
   513		where the first equality follows from~\eqref{eq:lc-23} and for the second line we used the approximate (anti-)commutation
   514	        relation~\eqref{eq:pts-obs-commutation} for the
   515	        $X^{r_\xpt}(u_\xpt)$ and  $Z^{r_\zpt}(u_\zpt)$
   516	        observables, as well as the exact (anti-)commutation relations
   517	        for the $\tau^Z(r_\zpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\zpt))$ and
   518	        $\tau^X(r_\xpt \cdot \ind_m(u_\xpt))$ observables. This shows
   519	        the desired approximate commutation relation, with
   520	        $\delta_{\acom} = \sqrt{\eps}$.
   521	\end{proof}
   522	
   523	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-comm-line-cons}
   524	There exists a function $\delta_{\Line}(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   525		For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and lines $\line$ there exists a projective measurement $\{ \hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f \}_{f \in \deg_{md}(\line)}$, acting on registers $\alice\alice'$ or $\bob\alice''$, such that:
   526		\begin{enumerate}
   527			\item  (\textbf{Self-consistency})\label{enu:qld-comm-line-self-cons}  For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $r \in \F_q$, on average over a uniformly random  pair $(\line, u)$
   528	                drawn from the line-point distribution
   529	                (\Cref{def:line-point-dist}),
   530			\[
   531				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line} (\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   532			\]
   533			
   534			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements I}) \label{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons}
   535			On average over a uniformly random pair $(\line, u)$
   536	                drawn from the line-point distribution, 
   537			\[
   538				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line} (\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{f(u)})_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   539			\]		
   540			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements II}) \label{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons2}
   541			On average over a uniformly random pair $(\line, u)$
   542	                drawn from the line-point distribution,
   543			\[
   544				(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) = a]})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_\Line}  (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{a})_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   545			\]
   546	              \end{enumerate}
   547	                    Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   548	      also hold.
   549	\end{lemma}
   550	
   551	\begin{proof}
   552		Define the operator
   553		\[
   554			\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f = \sum_{\substack{f',f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line) : \\ f' + f'' = f}} M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{f'} \otimes \tau^{W,\line}_{f''}\;,
   555		\]
   556		where the Pauli operator $\tau^{W,\line}_{f''}$ acting on register $\alice'$ is obtained by measuring all $\nqubits$ qudits in the basis $W$ to obtain an outcome $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ and then returning the restriction $f''$ of $g_h: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ to the line $\line$. Here, $g_h$ is the degree-$d$ low-degree extension of $h$ defined in~\eqref{eq:ld-encoding}. 
   557		
   558		\Cref{enu:qld-comm-line-self-cons},	the self-consistency of $\{\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f \}$, follows from the fact that the original lines measurement $\{ M^{(\Line,W),\line}_f \}$ is self-consistent between registers $\alice$ and $\bob$ in $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ (\Cref{enu:qld-cons} in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications}), the Pauli projections $\{\tau^{W,\line}_{f''}\}$ are perfectly self-consistent on between registers $\alice'$ and $\alice''$, and~\Cref{fact:data-processing}. 
   559	
   560	\Cref{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons}, the consistency with the points measurements, follows because on average over $(\line,u)$ drawn from the line-point distribution we have
   561	\begin{align}
   562		&(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \\
   563		&= \sum_{\substack{f',f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line) : \\ f' + f'' =
   564	  f}} (M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{f'} \otimes \tau^{W,\line}_{f''})_{\alice
   565	  \alice'} \\
   566	        &= \sum_{\substack{f', f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line): \\ f' + f'' =
   567	  f}} ((M^{(\Line, W), \line}_{f'} \otimes \tau^{W, \line}_{f''})
   568	  \cdot (M^{(\Line, W), \line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) = f'(u)]} )_{\alice
   569	  \alice'} \label{eq:qld-mhat-line-1} \\
   570		&\approx_\eps \sum_{\substack{f',f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line) : \\
   571	  f' + f'' = f}} (M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{f'} \otimes
   572	  \tau^{W,\line}_{f''})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes
   573	  (M^{(\Point,W),u}_{f'(u)})_{\bob
   574	  \alice''} \label{eq:qld-mhat-line-2} \\
   575	  	&= \sum_{\substack{f',f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line) : \\ f' + f'' =
   576	  f}} (M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{f'} \otimes \tau^{W,\line}_{f''})_{\alice
   577	  \alice'} \otimes (M^{(\Point,W),u}_{f'(u)} \otimes
   578	  \tau^{W,u}_{f''(u)})_{\bob \alice''} \label{eq:qld-mhat-line-3} \\
   579		&= \sum_{\substack{f',f'' \in \deg_{md}(\line) : \\ f' + f'' =
   580	  f}} (M^{(\Line,W),\line}_{f'} \otimes \tau^{W,\line}_{f''})_{\alice
   581	  \alice'} \otimes \Big (\sum_{\substack{a', a'' : \\ a' + a'' = f'(u)
   582	  + f''(u)}}  M^{(\Point,W),u}_{a'} \otimes \tau^{W,u}_{a''} \Big
   583	  )_{\bob \alice''} \label{eq:qld-mhat-line-4} \\
   584		&= (\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_f)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes
   585	   (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{f(u)})_{\bob \alice''}\;. \label{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons-eps}
   586	\end{align}
   587	\Cref{eq:qld-mhat-line-1} follows from the projectivity of
   588	$\{\hat{M}^{(\Line, W), \line}_{f}\}$. \Cref{eq:qld-mhat-line-2} follows from the consistency between the line
   589	and point measurements (\Cref{enu:qld-ld} in
   590	Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications}) together with

   640	\begin{align*}

   648	\label{eq:qld-comm-line-2}

   650	      \end{equation}

   652	      projective measurements. For families of projective measurements $\{A^x_i\}$
   653	      and $\{B^x_i\}$ acting on separate registers of a bipartite state
   654	      $\ket{\phi}$, suppose $I \approx_{\delta} \sum_i A^x_i \ot B^x_i$. Then
   655	      \begin{align*}

   663	      the third line, to remove the square. Thus

   665	        \delta\;, \]

   667	      Item~1 of \Cref{fact:agreement}, this in turn implies that $A^x_i \ot I

   669	      measurements $\{ (\hat{M}^{(\Line, W), \line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) =
   670	        a]})_{\alice \alice'} \}_a$ and $\{(\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),
   671	        u}_{a})_{\bob \alice''}\}$ in~\eqref{eq:qld-comm-line-2} gives
   672	      \[
   673		(\hat{M}^{(\Line,W),\line}_{[\eval_u(\cdot) = a]})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\sqrt{\eps}} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,W),u}_{a})_{\bob \alice''}.
   674	      \]
   675	      Taking the function $\delta_{\Line}$ in the lemma to be $\sqrt{\eps}$,
   676	      this yields the conclusion of \Cref{eq:qld-comm-line-pt-cons2}
   677	      of the lemma.
   678	\end{proof}

   680	 \subsection{Combining the $X$ and $Z$ measurements}
   681	\label{sec:combining}
   682	
   683	In this section our goal is to create a set of combined measurements
   684	that simultaneously measure the approximately-commuting measurements
   685	constructed in the previous section. We do this first for the points.
   686	Recall that $\mH_\alice$ and $\mH_\bob$ denote the Hilbert spaces corresponding to
   687	registers $\alice$ and $\bob$, respectively.
   688	
   689	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   690	There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   691		For every $x,z \in \F_q^m$ and $\mH \in \{ \mH_\alice, \mH_\bob\}$ there are projective measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting on $\mathcal{H} \otimes (\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ such that:
   692		\begin{enumerate}
   693			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   694			\begin{equation}
   695				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   696				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'}  \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\bob \alice''}\,.
   697			\end{equation}
   698			
   699			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   700			\begin{gather}

701				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   702					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} \hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b)_{\bob \alice''}\;, \\
   703								\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   704					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b  \hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} )_{\bob \alice''}\;.
   705			\end{gather}
   706	              \end{enumerate}
   707	                    Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations
   708	      also hold.
   709	\end{lemma}
   710	
   711	The construction of the measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ whose existence is guaranteed in the lemma proceeds in three steps. In the first step, for every $(r,s)\in\F_q^2$ we combine the binary-outcome measurements $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x,r}_a$ and $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),z,s}_b$; this is made possible by their approximate commutation as shown in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}. In a second step, we show that the measurements thus constructed have a particular ``approximate linearity'' property, when seen as a function of the pair $(r,s)$. This allows us, in the third step, to combine them into a single measurement $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ with outcomes in $\F_q^2\cong \F_2^{2t}$ by applying the following  result from~\cite{NV17}:
   712		
   713		\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test]
   714		\label{thm:linearity}
   715			Let $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob$. Let $\{\mathcal{O}^u \}$ be a set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ that act on $\mathcal{H}_\alice$. Suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen uniformly from $\F_2^t$, we have the following ``approximate linearity'' holds:
   716			\[
   717	(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\alice} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\alice}
   718			\]
   719			where the $\approx$ statement is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$. 
   720	Then there exists an extended state $\ket{\psi'}_{\alice \alice' \bob} = \ket{\psi}_{\alice \bob} \otimes \ket{0}_{\alice'}$ in an extended space $\mathcal{H}_{\alice} \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ and observables $\{ \mathcal{L}^u \}$ acting on $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ such that for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, 
   721			\[
   722				\mathcal{L}^u \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u + u'} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\mathcal{L}^u)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^u)_\alice \,.
   723			\]
   724			Furthermore, the observable $\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ when $u = 0$.
   725		\end{theorem}
   726			
   727			We now give the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}.
   728			
   729	\begin{proof}[Proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}]
   730	For convenience in the proof we slightly abuse the notation $\approx_\delta$ to mean $\approx_{\poly(\eps)}$ for some polynomial function $\delta=\poly(\eps)$ that may differ each time the notation is used. 
   731	
   732	\textbf{First step: construction of projective binary measurements $\{ \hat{R}^\omega_{a,b} \}$.}

   735			\hat{R}^\omega_{a,b} = \hat{M}^{(\Point,\zpt),z,s}_{b} \cdot \hat{M}^{(\Point,\xpt),x,r}_{a} \cdot \hat{M}^{(\Point,\zpt),z,s}_{b} \,.

   750			&= 1\;. \notag
   751		\end{align}

   753		\begin{align*}

   968	      \subsection{Applying the classical low-degree test}
   969	      \label{sec:apply-ldt}
   970	      In the previous section we showed how to combine the
   971	      approximately commuting $X$ and $Z$ basis point and line
   972	      measurements into a joint point measurement and a joint line
   973	      measurement. In this section we show how these measurements can be combined
   974				in a single measurement
   975	      that returns a pair of global polynomials encoding the $X$-basis and
   976	      $Z$-basis information, respectively, by applying the lemma that states quantum soundness of the classical low-degree test, Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   977				
   978	      Introduce a ``combining'' map that
   979	      takes two polynomials $f, g \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and returns a new polynomial $\combine_{f,g} \in \ideg_{d,
   980	        2m+2}(\F_q)$ defined by
   981	      \[ \combine_{f,g}(\underbrace{x}_{\in \F_q^{m}},
   982	        \underbrace{z}_{\in \F_q^m}, \underbrace{\alpha}_{\in \F_q},
   983	        \underbrace{\beta}_{\in \F_q}) = \alpha f(x) + \beta g(z)\;. \]

   857	\begin{lemma}[The global polynomial-pair measurement]
   858		\label{lem:qld-4-7}
   859		\uses{def:polyfunc, def:expanded-state, def:expanded-point-measurement,
   860			def:consistency, def:bracket}
   861		There exists a function
   862		$\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$, for some
   863		universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that the following
   864		holds. For $\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there
   865		exists a projective measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ acting on
   866		$\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$, with outcomes consisting of pairs
   867		$(g_X, g_Z)$ of polynomials, each in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$, such
   868		that for $W \in \{X, Z\}$, on average over uniformly random
   869		$u \in \F_q^m$,
   870		\begin{align}
   871			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   872			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   873			&\simeq_{\delta_S}
   874			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a}
   875			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   876			\label{eq:qld-s-point-con-alice} \\
   877			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   878			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'}
   879			&\simeq_{\delta_S}
   880			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a}
   881			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,
   882			\label{eq:qld-s-point-con-bob}
   883		\end{align}
   884		where $\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W)$ denotes the evaluation at the point $u$
   885		of the first outcome $g_X$ if $W = X$, and of the second outcome $g_Z$
   886		if $W = Z$.
   887	\end{lemma}
   888	\begin{proof}
   889		\uses{lem:qld-4-13, lem:qld-4-12, thm:naimark, lem:ld-soundness,
   890			def:ld-game, fact:agreement, fact:add-a-proj2,
   891			fact:data-processing, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree,
   892			def:combine-map}
   893		By Lemmas~\ref{lem:qld-4-12} and~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}, the expanded state
   894		$\ket{\hat\psi}$ together with the lines measurements
   895		$\{\hat{Q}^{\ell}_{f}\}$ and the points measurements
   896		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\}$ constitutes a strategy for the
   897		classical low individual degree game (Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}) with
   898		parameters $(q, 2m+2, d, 1)$ succeeding with probability
   899		$1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$; the axis-parallel clause of
   900		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13} supplies the degree-$d$ answer format that the
   901		game requires on axis-parallel lines. Since $\{\hat{Q}^{\ell}_{f}\}$ is
   902		only a POVM, it is first made projective by Naimark dilation
   903		(Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), which preserves the $\simeq$ conclusions of
   904		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}. The quantum soundness of the classical test
   905		(Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, applied with $m$ replaced by $2m+2$ and
   906		$\eps$ by $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$) then yields a POVM
   907		$\{\hat{S}_g\}$ with outcomes $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,2m+2}(\F_q)$ that
   908		is $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$-self-consistent and
   909		$\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$-consistent with the points measurements
   910		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\}$, where
   911		$\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}
   912		= a(md)^a(\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$
   913		for universal constants $a, b$; a second application of Naimark dilation
   914		makes $\{\hat{S}_g\}$ projective with the same guarantees. Let
   915		$\mathcal{G}$ be the set of polynomials of the form
   916		$g(x,z,\alpha,\beta) = \alpha g_X(x) + \beta g_Z(z)$ with
   917		$g_X, g_Z \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. A chain of approximations
   918		built from the consistency of $\{\hat{S}_g\}$ with the points
   919		measurements and the relations
   920		\eqref{eq:qld-4-12-cons-m-hat}--\eqref{eq:qld-4-12-cons-m-hat2} of
   921		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-12} (using Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} to convert

   929		coefficient polynomials $g_1$ or $g_2$ depend on the wrong block of
   930		variables --- yields
   931		$\sum_{g \notin \mathcal{G}}
   932		\| (\hat{S}_g)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ket{\hat\psi} \|^2
   933		\le O(\delta_{\mathrm{ld}} + \delta_Q + md/q)
   934		=: \delta_{\mathcal{G}}$.

   936		$\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z} = \hat{S}_{\mathrm{combine}_{g_X,g_Z}}$
   937		(Definition~\ref{def:combine-map}); its incompleteness is at most
   938		$\delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, and a further approximation chain with
   939		successive errors $\delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, $\delta_Q^{1/2}$,
   940		$\delta_Q^{1/2}$, $1/q$, $1/q$ gives
   941		\[
   942			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_x(\cdot) = a,\
   943				\mathrm{eval}_z(\cdot) = b]}
   944			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   945			\simeq_{O(\delta_{\mathcal{G}} + \delta_Q^{1/2} + 1/q)}
   946			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}\,
   947			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}\,
   948			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}
   949			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   950		\]

   952		$\Id - \sum_{g_X,g_Z} \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}$ to an arbitrary element costs a
   953		further $\delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, and the resulting error
   954		$\delta_S = O(\delta_{\mathrm{ld}} + \delta_Q^{1/2} + md/q)$ has the
   955		stated form for suitable universal constants; an application of
   956		Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing} then gives
   957		\eqref{eq:qld-s-point-con-alice} for $W = X$. For $W = Z$ the same

   959		opposite-order correlation, and entirely analogous calculations with
   960		the registers swapped yield \eqref{eq:qld-s-point-con-bob}.
   961	\end{proof}

    56	\section{Combined point measurements}
    57	
    58	The measurements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}$ and
    59	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}$ commute only approximately. The first goal of
    60	this chapter is to construct a single projective measurement that
    61	simultaneously measures both, first at points and then along lines. The
    62	construction of the combined point measurement proceeds in three steps: the
    63	binary refinements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}$ and
    64	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}$ are combined into a sandwich POVM, the
    65	resulting family is shown to satisfy an approximate linearity in the index
    66	pair $(r,s)$, and the following result of Natarajan and
    67	Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity} converts approximate linearity into exact
    68	linearity, from which a projective measurement with outcomes in $\F_q^2$ is
    69	assembled by Fourier averaging.
    70	
    71	\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
    72		\label{thm:linearity}
    73		\uses{def:povm-distance}
    74		Let $0 \le \delta \le 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let
    75		$\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space
    76		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}$. Let $\{\mathcal{O}^u\}$ be a
    77		set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
    78		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}$, and suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen
    79		uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$ the approximate linearity
    80		\[
    81			(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
    82			\approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
    83		\]
    84		holds with respect to $\ket{\psi}$. Then there exist an extended state
    85		$\ket{\psi'}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{B}}
    86		= \ket{\psi}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}} \ot \ket{0}_{\mathsf{A}'}$
    87		in an extended space
    88		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{B}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ and
    89		observables $\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ acting on
    90		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ such that for all
    91		$u, u' \in \F_2^t$,
    92		\[
    93			\mathcal{L}^u \, \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}
    94			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
    95			(\mathcal{L}^u)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
    96			\approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^u)_{\mathsf{A}}\,,
    97		\]
    98		the latter with respect to $\ket{\psi'}$. Furthermore,
    99		$\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ when $u = 0$.
   100	\end{theorem}
   101	\begin{proof}
   102		This is the quantum linearity test of Natarajan and
   103		Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}; no proof is given in
   104		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, which invokes the result directly. The statement is
   105		imported here as an external result; see
   106		Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-import}.
   107	\end{proof}

   114		the statement are load-bearing for the proof of
   115		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the error is preserved exactly ($\delta$ in the
   116		hypothesis equals $\delta$ in the conclusion), and the linearity of the
   117		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ is exact and holds for all pairs $(u,u')$, not merely
   118		on average.
   119	\end{remark}

   121	\begin{lemma}[Combined point measurements]

   162	\begin{proof}

   166		Throughout the proof every intermediate error is a $\poly(\eps)$ function

   168		$\omega = (x,z,r,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q$
   169		and $a, b \in \F_2$ define the sandwich POVM
   170		$\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b}
   171		= \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}_{b}
   172		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}_{a}
   173		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}_{b}$

   683	In this section our goal is to create a set of combined measurements
   684	that simultaneously measure the approximately-commuting measurements
   685	constructed in the previous section. We do this first for the points.

   689	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   690	There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the following holds. 
   691		For every $x,z \in \F_q^m$ and $\mH \in \{ \mH_\alice, \mH_\bob\}$ there are projective measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting on $\mathcal{H} \otimes (\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ such that:
   692		\begin{enumerate}
   693			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   694			\begin{equation}
   695				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   696				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'}  \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\bob \alice''}\,.
   697			\end{equation}
   698			
   699			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly random $x,z \in \F_q^m$,
   700			\begin{gather}
   701				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   702					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} \hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b)_{\bob \alice''}\;, \\
   703								\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   704					(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\alice \alice'} \approx_{\delta_Q} (\hat{M}^{(\Point,Z),z}_b  \hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x}_{a} )_{\bob \alice''}\;.

   706	              \end{enumerate}

   708	      also hold.

   711	The construction of the measurements $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ whose existence is guaranteed in the lemma proceeds in three steps. In the first step, for every $(r,s)\in\F_q^2$ we combine the binary-outcome measurements $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),x,r}_a$ and $\hat{M}^{(\Point,X),z,s}_b$; this is made possible by their approximate commutation as shown in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}. In a second step, we show that the measurements thus constructed have a particular ``approximate linearity'' property, when seen as a function of the pair $(r,s)$. This allows us, in the third step, to combine them into a single measurement $\{ \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b} \}$ with outcomes in $\F_q^2\cong \F_2^{2t}$ by applying the following  result from~\cite{NV17}:
   712		
   713		\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test]
   714		\label{thm:linearity}
   715			Let $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let $\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob$. Let $\{\mathcal{O}^u \}$ be a set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ that act on $\mathcal{H}_\alice$. Suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen uniformly from $\F_2^t$, we have the following ``approximate linearity'' holds:
   716			\[
   717	(\mathcal{O}^u \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\alice} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\alice}
   718			\]
   719			where the $\approx$ statement is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$. 
   720	Then there exists an extended state $\ket{\psi'}_{\alice \alice' \bob} = \ket{\psi}_{\alice \bob} \otimes \ket{0}_{\alice'}$ in an extended space $\mathcal{H}_{\alice} \otimes \mathcal{H}_\bob \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ and observables $\{ \mathcal{L}^u \}$ acting on $\mathcal{H}_\alice \otimes \mathcal{H}_{\alice'}$ such that for all $u, u' \in \F_2^t$, 
   721			\[
   722				\mathcal{L}^u \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u + u'} \qquad \text{and} \qquad (\mathcal{L}^u)_{\alice \alice'} \approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^u)_\alice \,.
   723			\]
   724			Furthermore, the observable $\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ when $u = 0$.
   725		\end{theorem}

   857	\begin{lemma}[The global polynomial-pair measurement]

   862		$\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$, for some

   865		exists a projective measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ acting on
   866		$\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$, with outcomes consisting of pairs
   867		$(g_X, g_Z)$ of polynomials, each in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$, such
   868		that for $W \in \{X, Z\}$, on average over uniformly random
   869		$u \in \F_q^m$,
   870		\begin{align}
   871			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   872			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   873			&\simeq_{\delta_S}

   877			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   878			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'}
   879			&\simeq_{\delta_S}
   880			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a}

   882			\label{eq:qld-s-point-con-bob}

   888	\begin{proof}
   889		\uses{lem:qld-4-13, lem:qld-4-12, thm:naimark, lem:ld-soundness,
   890			def:ld-game, fact:agreement, fact:add-a-proj2,
   891			fact:data-processing, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree,
   892			def:combine-map}
   893		By Lemmas~\ref{lem:qld-4-12} and~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}, the expanded state
   894		$\ket{\hat\psi}$ together with the lines measurements
   895		$\{\hat{Q}^{\ell}_{f}\}$ and the points measurements
   896		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\}$ constitutes a strategy for the
   897		classical low individual degree game (Definition~\ref{def:ld-game}) with
   898		parameters $(q, 2m+2, d, 1)$ succeeding with probability
   899		$1 - \delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$; the axis-parallel clause of
   900		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13} supplies the degree-$d$ answer format that the
   901		game requires on axis-parallel lines. Since $\{\hat{Q}^{\ell}_{f}\}$ is
   902		only a POVM, it is first made projective by Naimark dilation
   903		(Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}), which preserves the $\simeq$ conclusions of
   904		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}. The quantum soundness of the classical test
   905		(Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}, applied with $m$ replaced by $2m+2$ and
   906		$\eps$ by $\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}$) then yields a POVM
   907		$\{\hat{S}_g\}$ with outcomes $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,2m+2}(\F_q)$ that

   910		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\}$, where
   911		$\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}

   914		makes $\{\hat{S}_g\}$ projective with the same guarantees. Let
   915		$\mathcal{G}$ be the set of polynomials of the form
   916		$g(x,z,\alpha,\beta) = \alpha g_X(x) + \beta g_Z(z)$ with
   917		$g_X, g_Z \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. A chain of approximations
   918		built from the consistency of $\{\hat{S}_g\}$ with the points

   930		variables --- yields
   931		$\sum_{g \notin \mathcal{G}}
   932		\| (\hat{S}_g)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ket{\hat\psi} \|^2
   933		\le O(\delta_{\mathrm{ld}} + \delta_Q + md/q)
   934		=: \delta_{\mathcal{G}}$.

   937		(Definition~\ref{def:combine-map}); its incompleteness is at most
   938		$\delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, and a further approximation chain with

   940		$\delta_Q^{1/2}$, $1/q$, $1/q$ gives

   947			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}\,
   948			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}
   949			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   950		\]

   953		further $\delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, and the resulting error

1415	 \subsection{Pulling the $X$ and $Z$ measurements apart}
  1416	\label{sec:separating}
  1417	
  1418	
  1419	Recall the decoding map of the low-degree code defined in \Cref{sec:ld-encoding}. This map takes in a polynomial $g \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and returns a string $\coded(g) \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$ consisting of the evaluations of $g$ on the points in the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$.
  1420	We now use this decoding map to construct a new set of measurement operators out of $\hat{S}$.
  1421	First, we introduce some notation. For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and all degree $d$ polynomials $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ define projectors
  1422	\[ \hat{S}^X_g = \sum_{g_\zpt} \hat{S}_{g,g_\zpt} \quad  \text{and}  \quad \hat{S}^Z_g = \sum_{g_\xpt} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g}\;,\]
  1423	where the measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is given by \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}.
  1424	
  1425	For all $W \in \{X, Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{\nqubits}$, and $a \in \F_q$, define the projector
  1426	\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tauwu}
  1427	 \tau^{W}_{a}(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{\nqubits} \,:\, h \cdot \tilde{u} = a} \tau^W_{h}
  1428	\end{equation}
  1429	where recall that $\tau^W_h$ is the projector corresponding to measuring $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$ in the $W$ basis and obtaining $h \in \F_q^\nqubits$ as the outcome. For all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$ define the projective measurement $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}_{a \in \F_q}$ by 
  1430		\begin{equation}
  1431		\label{eq:tilde_M}
  1432		\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a =  \sum_{g} \hat{S}^W_g \otimes \tau_{(\coded(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a}^W(\tilde{u})\;.
  1433		\end{equation}
  1434		If $\hat{S}^W_g$ is viewed as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice'$ (resp. $\bob \bob'$) then we view $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ as an operator acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ (resp. $\bob \bob' \bob''$). (When necessary we will indicate via subscripts which registers the operators are acting on.)
  1435	The $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ are projective because the $\hat{S}^W_g$ and $\tau^W$ operators are projective.
  1436	
  1437	
  1438		For all $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ define the observable
  1439		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tildewj}
  1440			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) = \sum_a (-1)^{\tr(e_j a)} \, \tilde{M}_a^{W,\tilde{u}} \;,
  1441		\end{equation}
  1442		where $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ denotes the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ specified in \Cref{sec:subfields}. Let $\tau^W$ be the generalized Pauli observable defined in Section~\ref{sec:generalized-pauli}. Observe that
  1443		\begin{align*}
  1444		\Big ( \sum_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \Big ) \otimes \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})
  1445		&= \sum_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \sum_h (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} (-1)^{\tr(e_j(\tilde{u} \cdot h))} \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \otimes \tau^W_h\\
  1446		&= \sum_{g_W} \sum_a  (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\tilde{u} \cdot\coded(g_W) + a))} \hat{S}_{g_W}^W \otimes \Big( \sum_{h:\, h\cdot \tilde{u} = a}\tau^W_h\Big)\\
  1447			&= \sum_{g_W} \sum_a  (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\tilde{u} \cdot\coded(g_W) + a))} \hat{S}_{g_W}^W \otimes \tau^W_a(\tilde{u})\\
  1448			&= 		\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \;,
  1449		\end{align*}
  1450		where the first equality uses the definition of $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$, the second uses the definition of $\hat{S}^W_{g_W}$ and regroups terms, the third uses the definition~\eqref{eq:def-tauwu} of $\tau^W_a(\tilde{u})$, and the last is by a change of variables.   1451		Furthermore, it can be verified by direct calculation that the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the same relations as the generalized Pauli group. Specifically, for all $j,j' \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \F_q^\nqubits$,
  1452		\[
  1453			\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) \tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v}) = \begin{cases}
  1454			\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v}) \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})  & \qquad j \neq j' \\
  1455			(-1)^{\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_j \tilde{v}))} \tilde{Z}^{j}(\tilde{v}) \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) & \qquad j = j'

  1457		\]
  1458		The next lemma shows that the measurements $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}$  and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$  are consistent with the original points measurements, and are self-consistent.

  1463	\begin{lemma}
  1464	  \label{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}
  1465	Let $\delta_S$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}.
  1466	For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, all $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$ and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, the measurements $\{ \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \}_{a \in \F_q}$ and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the following properties:
  1467	\begin{enumerate}
  1468	\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, for all $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, and on average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$,
  1469		\[
  1470			\Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes \tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \simeq_{\delta_S} M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''}
  1471		\]
  1472		and
  1473		\[
  1474			\tilde{M}^{W,\ind_m(u)}_a \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes M^{(\Point,W),u}_a \;.
  1475		\]	
  1476		\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits$,
  1477		\[
  1478			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id_{\bob \bob' \bob''} \approx_{\delta_S} \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''} \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})\,.
  1479		\]
  1480	\end{enumerate}

  1483	\begin{proof}

   396		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   397		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   398		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   399		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if

   405	\section{Lines}
   406	
   407	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   408	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   409	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   410	
   411	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   412		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   413		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   414		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   415			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   416		\end{equation}
   417		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   418		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   419		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   420		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   421		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   422		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   423		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   424		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   425	\end{definition}
   426	
   427	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   428		\uses{def:line}
   429		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   430		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   431	\end{proposition}
   432	\begin{proof}
   433		\uses{def:line}
   434		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   435		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   436		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   437		inclusion.
   438	\end{proof}
   439	
   440	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   441	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   442	representation is obtained as follows.
   443	
   444	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   445		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   446		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   447		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   448		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   449		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   450		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   451		\[
   452			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   453		\]
   454		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   455		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   456		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   457		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   458		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   459		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   460		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   461		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   462		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   463		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   464	\end{definition}

   832	\subsection{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   833	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   834	
   835	In this section, we introduce some basic definitions about polynomials over finite fields. 
   836	An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   837	\[
   838		f(x_1,\ldots,x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0,1,\ldots,q-1\}^m} c_\alpha
   839	  x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   840	\]
   841	where $\{c_\alpha\}$ is a collection of coefficients in $\F_q$.
   842	We say that $f$ has \emph{individual degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if
   843	$\alpha_i \leq d $ for all $1\leq i\leq m$, and that it has \emph{total degree
   844	  (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha\neq 0$ only if $\sum_i \alpha_i \leq d$.
   845	(Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials are polynomials with individual degree
   846	$1$.
   847	
   848	Low-degree polynomials play an important role in this paper.
   849	For one, the classical and quantum low-degree tests of \Cref{sec:ldt} are
   850	nonlocal games that efficiently certify that the players' answers are consistent
   851	with low-degree polynomials.
   852	Low-degree polynomials are also crucial in the probabilistically checkable
   853	proofs (PCP) construction that are used in ``answer reduction'' transformation
   854	(\Cref{sec:ans}).
   855	
   856	We recall the Schwartz-Zippel lemma: 
   857	
   858	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz-Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]
   859	  \label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   860	  Let $f, g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials with total degree at most $d$. Then
   861	  \begin{equation*}
   862	    \Pr_{x \sim \F_q^m}[f(x) = g(x)] \leq d/q\;.
   863	  \end{equation*}
   864	\end{lemma}
   865	
   866	
   867	\paragraph{The low-degree code.}
   868	The Schwartz-Zippel lemma implies that the set of low-degree polynomials form an
   869	error-correcting code with good distance, which we call the \emph{low-degree
   870	  code}.\footnote{It is also known as the \emph{generalized Reed-Muller code} in
   871	  the coding theory literature.}
   872	
   873	Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$.
   874	For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ define the following $m$-variate multilinear
   875	polynomial over $\F_q$:
   876	\[
   877		\ind_{m,y}(x) = \prod_{i: y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i: y_i = 0} (1 - x_i) \;.
   878	\]
   879	Here, we identify $\{0,1\}$ as a subset of $\F_q$.
   880	Notice that, when restricted to the subcube $\{0,1\}^m$, $\ind_{m, y}$ is zero
   881	everywhere except for when $x = y$.
   882	For $a\in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y\in \{0,1\}^m$
   883	(identifying the latter set with $\{1,\ldots,M\}$ using, say, the lexicographic
   884	ordering on strings).
   885	For any such $a$ define the multilinear polynomial $g_a: \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   886	called the \emph{low-degree encoding of $a$}, as follows:
   887	\begin{equation}
   888	\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   889		 g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)\;.
   890	\end{equation}
   891	Note that for any $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, $g_a(y) = a_y$.
   892	Furthermore, the map $a\mapsto g_a$ is linear: for every $x \in \F_q^m$,
   893	\begin{equation}
   894	\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   895		g_a(x) = a \cdot \ind_m(x)\;,
   896	\end{equation}
   897	where $\ind_m(x)$ is the vector $(\ind_{m,y}(x))_{y \in \{0,1\}^m}\in\F_q^M$.
   898	
   899	\begin{lemma}
   900	\label{lem:ld-encoding-complexity}
   901	Let $q$ be an admissible field size, and let $M = 2^m$ for some integer $m$.
   902	The complexity of computing the evaluation of the low-degree encoding $g_a(x)$,
   903	given $a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$ represented in binary, is $\poly(M,\log
   904	q)$.
   905	\end{lemma}
   906	\begin{proof}
   907		Computing $g_a(x)$ requires computing the sum of products $a_y \cdot
   908	  \ind_{m,y}(x)$ over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$.
   909	  Via \Cref{lem:efficient_arithmetic}, evaluating $\ind_{m,y}(x)$ takes time
   910	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ because it requires performing $m$ multiplications of $\F_q$
   911	  elements, and therefore the product $a_y \cdot \ind_{m,y}(x)$ requires
   912	  $\poly(m,\log q)$ time.
   913	  Computing the sum over all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ requires $M \cdot \poly(m,\log q)
   914	  = \poly(M,\log q)$ time, as claimed.
   915	\end{proof}
   916	
   917	Finally, for any $H \subseteq \F_q$ we define the \emph{decoding} map
   918	$\coded_H(\cdot)$ which takes as input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and
   919	returns the following vector $a \in \F_q^M$: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, if $g(y)
   920	\in H$, then set $a_y = g(y)$, and otherwise set $a_y = 0$.
   921	Note that for all $a \in H^M$ we have $\coded_H(g_a) = a$ where $g_a$ is the
   922	low-degree encoding of $a$.
   923	For notational brevity we often write $\coded(\cdot)$ to denote the boolean
   924	decoding map $\coded_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.

   353	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   354		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   355		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   356		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   357		\[
   358			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   359			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   360		\]
   361		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   362		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   363		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   364		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   365		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   366		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   367		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   368		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   369			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   370		\end{equation}
   371		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   372		degree at most $m$.

   375	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   376		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   377		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   378		\[
   379			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   380			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   381		\]
   382		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   383		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   384		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   385		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   386			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   387		\end{equation}
   388		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   389	\end{definition}
   390	
   391	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   392	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   393	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   394	
   395	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   396		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   397		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   398		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   399		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   400		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   401		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   402		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   403	\end{definition}

   171	\paragraph{Description complexity bounds.} When we bound the description lengths of
   172	the Turing machines presented in this paper, we do not worry about the exact
   173	details of how Turing machines are represented as binary strings -- as mentioned we assume that
   174	\emph{some} reasonable encoding is used -- but instead
   175	we distinguish between whether the Turing machine 
   176	description depends on any parameters used elsewhere in the paper. Note that whether the \emph{description} depends on any parameters is different from whether the Turing machine takes parameters as \emph{input}. For example, consider the following (high-level) descriptions of Turing machines $\cal{A}$ and $\cal{B}$:
   177	
   178	\begin{enumerate}
   179		\item Turing machine $\cal{A}$ takes two inputs $(\alpha,x)$ and outputs the integer $\alpha \times x$ where $\alpha, x$ are interpreted as positive integers written in binary. 
   180		\item Turing machine $\cal{B}$ takes one input $x$ and outputs the integer $\beta \times x$ where $\beta$ is a fixed positive integer.
   181	\end{enumerate}
   182	
   183	The description of $\cal{A}$ does not depend on any ``external'' parameters, so its description length $|\desc{\cal{A}}|$ is some universal constant, which we express as $O(1)$. On the other hand, the description of $\cal{B}$ depends on some fixed integer $\beta$; in other words, the parameter $\beta$ is ``hard-wired'' into $\cal{B}$'s description. The description of $\cal{B}$ can be taken to be the following: $\cal{B}$ (which is a $1$-input Turing machine) simulates the execution of the $2$-input Turing machine $\cal{A}$ where the first input tape of $\cal{A}$ has the binary representation of $\beta$ written onto it and the second input tape has $x$ (which is provided as input to $B$) written into it. Thus the description of $\cal{B}$ includes the binary representation of $\beta$, the description of $\cal{A}$ (whose length is a universal constant), and the description of the universal Turing machine (whose length is a universal constant). Thus the description length of $\cal{B}$ is $O(\log \beta) + O(1) = O(\log \beta)$.
   184	
   185	
   186	
   187	\paragraph{Time complexity bounds.} When we bound the time complexity of the Turing machines presented in this paper, we similarly do not worry about the exact
   188	implementation details, but instead we assume that basic computations such as integer arithmetic, string comparisons, etc.\ are all performed
   189	using reasonably efficient algorithms that run in polynomial time in the length of the input. When running other Turing machines as subroutines, we assume that there is some polynomial overhead due to \Cref{thm:universal-tm}.
   190	
   191	
   192	\paragraph{Timeout counters.} We sometimes define Turing machines that are required to halt if 
   193	either the Turing machine or some subroutine takes a number of time steps that exceeds some specified threshold. For example, we may write ``Let $\cal{M}$ be the Turing machine that on input the description $\ol{\cal{R}}$ of a Turing machine $\cal{R}$ and an integer $T$, simulates $\cal{R}$ on the empty tape and halts if more than $T$ steps are performed.''
   194	
   195	This is useful for establishing an \emph{a priori} bound on the time complexity of the Turing machine. In particular we will be able to claim that $\cal{M}$, as described above, always runs in time at most $\poly(T,|\ol{\cal{R}}|$, irrespective of the running time of $\cal{R}$ itself.
   196	
   197	We explain how such a Turing machine can be realized formally. We use a variant of the universal Turing machine of \Cref{thm:universal-tm}. Using the theorem, it is straightforward to show that given a (single tape) Turing machine $\cal{R}$ there exists another two-tape Turing machine $\cal{M}'$ such that, whenever the second tape is initialized to the binary representation of $T$, $\cal{M}'$ simulates $\cal{R}$ and in-between every simulated step of $\cal{R}$, decrements the second tape and checks if it reaches zero. If it does, then $\cal{M}'$ halts and rejects. Otherwise, it continues. 
   198	
   199	The time complexity of $\cal{M}'$ is, by definition, at most $O(T \log T)$ for all inputs. The description length of $\cal{M}'$ is at most $O(|\ol{\cal{R}}|)$, because this is the description size of the universal Turing machine, whose initial tape has been hardwired with $\ol{\cal{R}}$.
   200	To convert back to a single tape Turing machine and obtain $\cal{M}$ from $\cal{M}$' we can use \Cref{thm:universal-tm} again, at the cost of a polynomial blow-up in the time complexity.
   201	
   202	
   203	\paragraph{Input representations.} 
   204	Although the inputs and outputs of a Turing machine are strictly speaking
   205	  binary strings, we oftentimes slightly abuse notation and specify Turing
   206	  machines that treat their inputs and outputs as objects with more structure,
   207	  such as finite field elements, integers, symbols from a larger alphabet, and
   208	  so on.
   209	  In this case we implicitly assume that the Turing machine specification uses a
   210	  consistent convention to represent these structured objects as binary strings.
   211	  Conventions for objects such as integers are straightforward.
   212	  For representations of finite field elements, we refer the reader to
   213	  Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.

   219	Linear spaces considered in the paper generally take the form $V = \F^n$ for a
   220	finite field $\F$ and integer $n \geq 1$.
   221	In particular, when we write ``let $V$ be a linear space'', unless explicitly
   222	stated otherwise we always mean a space of the form $\F^n$.
   223	Let $\hat{E} = \{ \hat{e}_1, \hat{e}_2, \ldots, \hat{e}_n\}$ denote the standard basis of $V$, where for
   224	$i \in\{ 1, 2, \ldots, n\}$,
   225	\begin{equation*}
   226	  \hat{e}_i = (0, \ldots, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)
   227	\end{equation*}
   228	has a $1$ in the $i$-th coordinate and $0$'s elsewhere.

   230	itself.

   234	    is meant to create an analogy for how the space of multiple qubits is often
   235	    partitioned into ``registers'' containing a few qubits each.}

   238	  $V$ then $S = \text{span}\{\hat{e}_i|\,u_i=1\}$.

    80	$S = \mathrm{span}\{(1,1)\}$ has the distinct complements
    81	$\mathrm{span}\{(1,0)\}$ and $\mathrm{span}\{(0,1)\}$. Given a basis of $S$,

    84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace, and it
    98		depends on the set $F$ and not only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$. If $S$ is a
    99		register subspace spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the
   100		canonical complement of $\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its
   101		span coincides with $S^\perp$.
   102	\end{definition}
   103	
   104	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   105		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   106		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   107		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   108		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   109		\[
   110			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   111		\]
   112	\end{lemma}
   113	\begin{proof}
   114		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   115		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   116		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   117		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   118		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   119		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   120		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   121		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   122		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   123	\end{proof}

   306	\begin{definition}

   309	  Let $F = \{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly
   310	  independent vectors in $V$.

   312	  vectors defined as follows.
   313	  Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i, j}\, \hat{e}_j$.
   314		Using a canonical algorithm for Gaussian elimination that works over arbitrary

   316	  form $(b_{i, j})$.

   318	  of $(b_{i, j})$.

405	\section{Lines}
   406	
   407	The question distributions of the classical low individual degree game and of
   408	the Pauli basis test (Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}) sample lines in $\F_q^m$;
   409	we record here the definition of lines and their canonical representatives.
   410	
   411	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   412		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   413		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   414		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   415			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   416		\end{equation}
   417		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   418		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   419		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   420		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   421		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   422		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   423		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   424		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   425	\end{definition}
   426	
   427	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:line-equiv}
   428		\uses{def:line}
   429		Let $u, v \in \F_q^m$. Then for all $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, we have
   430		$\ell(u,v) = \ell(u',v)$.
   431	\end{proposition}
   432	\begin{proof}
   433		\uses{def:line}
   434		Fix $u' \in \ell(u,v)$, so $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$. Any
   435		$a \in \ell(u,v)$ has the form $a = u + sv = u' + (s - t)v$, so
   436		$\ell(u,v) \subseteq \ell(u',v)$. The symmetric argument gives the reverse
   437		inclusion.
   438	\end{proof}
   439	
   440	Thus, for a fixed direction, a line is an equivalence class of its points: the
   441	pair $(u,v)$ representing it can use any base point on the line. A canonical
   442	representation is obtained as follows.
   443	
   444	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]\label{def:line-representative}
   445		\uses{def:line, def:cl-canonical, prop:line-equiv}
   446		Let $\ell$ be a line in direction $v \neq 0$, and let
   447		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v : \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with
   448		the one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$
   449		(Definition~\ref{def:cl-canonical}). The \emph{canonical representative of
   450		$\ell$} is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   451		\[
   452			u_0 = L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u) \qquad \text{for all } u \in \ell\;.
   453		\]
   454		This is well defined: since the image and kernel of $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$ are
   455		complementary, any $u \in \ell$ decomposes uniquely as $u = u_0 + tv$ with
   456		$u_0$ in the image, so $u_0 = u - tv \in \ell$ and
   457		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v(u_0) = u_0$; moreover any two points of $\ell$ differ by
   458		a multiple of $v$ and therefore have the same image under
   459		$L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_v$. A line $\ell = \ell(u,v)$ is henceforth canonically
   460		represented by the pair $(u_0, v)$. (For $v = 0$, where the singleton
   461		$\{u\}$ leaves no independent kernel basis, we take $L^{\mathrm{Ln}}_0$ to
   462		be the identity---the canonical linear map with empty kernel basis---so
   463		that $u_0 = u$; the source leaves this case implicit.)
   464	\end{definition}

   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}

   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}

   446	\begin{definition}[Restricted line distributions]
   447		\label{def:ith-restricted-line}
   448		\uses{def:line-point-dist, def:ld-question-distribution}

   450		axis-parallel line distribution} $D_{\mathrm{ALine},i}$ is the
   451		restriction of $D_{\mathrm{ALine}}$ to pairs $(\ell, u)$ where the line
   452		$\ell$ is along the direction $e_i$, i.e.\ is of the form
   453		$\ell = (u_0, e_i)$. Similarly, the \emph{$i$-th restricted diagonal line
   454		distribution} $D_{\mathrm{DLine},i}$ is the restriction of
   455		$D_{\mathrm{DLine}}$ to pairs $(\ell, u)$ where the line
   456		$\ell = (u_0, s, v)$ satisfies $\chi(s) = i$ and coordinates
   457		$1, \dots, i-1$ of $v$ are $0$. (The function $\chi$ is the one used in

   462	\begin{lemma}[Restricted line distributions and error inflation]
   463		\label{lem:restricted-line-mixture-bounds}
   464		% This node corresponds to unlabelled prose in the source (the discussion

   471		$D_{\mathrm{DLine},i}$. As a consequence:

   474			distribution $D_{\mathrm{Line}}$ with error $\delta$ holds over each

   478			$D_{\mathrm{Line}} \times D_{\mathrm{Line}}$ holds over any product

   541		\uses{def:line-representative, def:ld-question-distribution,
   542			def:line-point-dist, def:ith-restricted-line}
   543		The distribution $D$ is described by a sampling procedure. First sample
   544		$(\ell, u)$ from the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and write
   545		$u = (u_X, u_Z, \alpha, \beta)$, so that Property~1 holds by
   546		construction. If $\ell$ is axis-parallel, $\ell = (v, e_j)$ with
   547		$v = (v_X, v_Z, \alpha_0, \beta_0)$, set
   548		$\ell_X = (v'_X, e_{i_X})$ and $\ell_Z = (v'_Z, e_{i_Z})$ where: for
   549		$1 \le j \le m$, $i_X = j$ and $i_Z$ is uniformly random in
   550		$\{1,\dots,m\}$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, $i_X$ is uniformly random and
   551		$i_Z = j - m$; for $2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $i_X$ and $i_Z$ are
   552		uniformly random; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are the canonical line
   553		representatives of $v_X, v_Z$ for the chosen directions
   554		(Definition~\ref{def:line-representative}), so that $v_X \in \ell_X$
   555		and $v_Z \in \ell_Z$. If $\ell$ is diagonal, $\ell = (v, s, w)$ with
   556		direction $w = (w_X, w_Z, \gamma, \delta)$ whose first nonzero
   557		coordinate has index $j = \chi(s)$, sample
   558		$\ell_X = (v'_X, s_X, w'_X)$ and $\ell_Z = (v'_Z, s_Z, w'_Z)$ where: for
   559		$1 \le j \le m$, $w'_X = w_X$ and $w'_Z = w_Z$ with $s_X, s_Z$ chosen so
   560		that $\chi(s_X) = j$ and $\chi(s_Z) = 1$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$,
   561		$w'_X$ is a uniformly random diagonal direction (with $s_X$ chosen
   562		accordingly) and $w'_Z = w_Z$ with $\chi(s_Z) = j - m$; for
   563		$2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both directions are uniformly random with
   564		$s_X, s_Z$ chosen accordingly; and again $v'_X, v'_Z$ are the canonical
   565		representatives. In each case a uniformly random point $u$ on $\ell$
   566		projects to a uniformly random point $u_X$ on $\ell_X$ (resp.\ $u_Z$ on
   567		$\ell_Z$), and a case analysis over $j$ shows that the marginal over
   568		$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is a mixture of the required product distributions:
   569		for instance, in the axis-parallel case with $1 \le j \le m$, the
   570		marginal over $(\ell_X, u_X)$ conditioned on $j$ equals
   571		$D_{\mathrm{ALine},j}$, and even conditioned on $(\ell_X, u_X)$ the line
   572		$\ell_Z$ is distributed as $D_{\mathrm{ALine},i_Z}$ for uniformly random
   573		$i_Z$; the remaining cases are analogous, differing only in how the
   574		indices are chosen. This gives Property~2. Property~3 is immediate from
   575		the procedure: when $\ell$ is axis-parallel, both $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$
   576		are constructed to be axis-parallel.
   577	\end{proof}

   596	\begin{lemma}[Replacing the combined point measurement by the ordered product]
   597		\label{lem:claim-17-1}

   599		% comment for cross-reference fidelity.

   601			def:expanded-point-measurement, def:expanded-state}
   602		\begin{align*}
   603			\E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   604			\E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   605			&\sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   606			\big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   607			\big(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   608			\ket{\hat\psi} \\
   609			\approx_{\delta_Q^{1/2}}\
   610			\E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   611			\E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   612			&\sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   613			\big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   614			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{f_Z(z)} \,
   615			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{f_X(x)}
   616			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}

   618		\end{align*}

   623		$W^{x,z}_{a,b} = \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}
   624		- \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}
   625		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}$

   627		sides. The first factor is at most $1$ because
   628		$\sum_{f_X,f_Z \,:\, f_X(x)=a,\ f_Z(z)=b}
   629		T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z} \le \Id$

   631		drawn from the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, a uniformly
   632		random point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ on $\ell$ is a uniformly random point
   633		of $\F_q^{2m+2}$, so the coordinates $x, z$ are independent and uniform
   634		in $\F_q^m$; hence

   636		\bra{\hat\psi} \Id \ot (W^{x,z}_{a,b})^2 \ket{\hat\psi}

   857	\begin{lemma}[The global polynomial-pair measurement]
   858		\label{lem:qld-4-7}
   859		\uses{def:polyfunc, def:expanded-state, def:expanded-point-measurement,
   860			def:consistency, def:bracket}
   861		There exists a function
   862		$\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$, for some
   863		universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$, such that the following
   864		holds. For $\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there
   865		exists a projective measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ acting on
   866		$\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$, with outcomes consisting of pairs
   867		$(g_X, g_Z)$ of polynomials, each in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$, such
   868		that for $W \in \{X, Z\}$, on average over uniformly random
   869		$u \in \F_q^m$,
   870		\begin{align}
   871			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   872			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   873			&\simeq_{\delta_S}
   874			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a}
   875			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   876			\label{eq:qld-s-point-con-alice} \\
   877			\big(\hat{S}_{[\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W) = a]}
   878			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'}
   879			&\simeq_{\delta_S}
   880			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a}
   881			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,
   882			\label{eq:qld-s-point-con-bob}
   883		\end{align}
   884		where $\mathrm{eval}_u(\cdot_W)$ denotes the evaluation at the point $u$
   885		of the first outcome $g_X$ if $W = X$, and of the second outcome $g_Z$
   886		if $W = Z$.
   887	\end{lemma}
   888	\begin{proof}
   889		\uses{lem:qld-4-13, lem:qld-4-12, thm:naimark, lem:ld-soundness,
   890			def:ld-game, fact:agreement, fact:add-a-proj2,
   891			fact:data-processing, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree,
   892			def:combine-map}
   893		By Lemmas~\ref{lem:qld-4-12} and~\ref{lem:qld-4-13}, the expanded state

     9	This chapter completes the analysis of the Pauli basis test~\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), $q = 2^t$, and $M = 2^m$ denotes the number of $q$-ary qudits tested for per player. (The letter $M$ also denotes measurement operators, always carrying super- and subscripts; the meaning is determined by context, as in the source.) We fix a projective strategy for the Pauli basis test game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability at least $1-\eps$, in the setting of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}: the shared state $\ket{\psi}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ is assumed padded with sufficiently many ancilla qubits in the state $\ket{0}$ (Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-setup}), and $\ket{\hat\psi}$ denotes the expanded state on the six registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, obtained by adjoining to each player the two halves of $M$ pairs $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-state}). Unless stated otherwise, every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement below is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\hat\psi}$, over the question distribution named in the statement, with register placements indicated by subscripts; ``all symmetric equivalents'' refers to the register interchanges of Remark~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}.
    10	
    11	We use the following objects from the preceding chapters: the combined point projectors $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ acting on the expanded space (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}); the projective polynomial-pair measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, with outcomes pairs of polynomials in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and error function
    12	\[
    13		\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\bigr)
    14	\]
    15	for universal constants $a > 1$, $0 < b < 1$; the decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}\colon \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q) \to \F_q^{M}$ of the low-degree code (Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}), which maps a polynomial $g$ to the string of its evaluations on the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$; and the low-degree encoding $h \mapsto g_h$ together with the vectors $\mathrm{ind}_m(u) \in \F_q^M$, characterized by $h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g_h(u)$ for all $u \in \F_q^m$ \eqref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}. The map $h \mapsto g_h$ is linear, and $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$.

    17	\section{The pulled-apart measurements and observables}

    19	The measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ reads out an $X$-polynomial and a $Z$-polynomial simultaneously. We now separate the two readings again, this time as commuting actions on distinct registers: the polynomial outcome is measured on the players' original registers, while a genuine Pauli measurement acts on the EPR register $\mathrm{A}''$ (resp.\ $\mathrm{B}''$).

    21	\begin{definition}[Single-basis marginals of the polynomial-pair measurement]\label{def:s-w-marginals}
    22		\uses{lem:qld-4-7}
    23		Let $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ be the projective measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}. For every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ define
    24		\[
    25			\hat{S}^X_g = \sum_{g_Z} \hat{S}_{g,g_Z}
    26			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
    27			\hat{S}^Z_g = \sum_{g_X} \hat{S}_{g_X,g}\;,
    28		\]
    29		the sums ranging over $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ is projective, its elements are mutually orthogonal projectors; hence each $\hat{S}^W_g$, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$, is a projector, and $\{\hat{S}^W_g\}_{g}$ is a projective measurement with outcomes in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$.
    30	\end{definition}
    31	
    32	\begin{definition}[Pauli dot-product projectors]\label{def:tau-dot-product-projector}
    33		\uses{def:generalized-pauli}
    34		For $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $h \in \F_q^{M}$ let $\tau^W_h$ denote the projector corresponding to measuring $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$ in the $W$ basis and obtaining the outcome $h$ (Definition~\ref{def:generalized-pauli}).
