    35		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tauwu}
    36			\tau^{W}_{a}(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{M} \,:\, h \cdot \tilde{u} = a} \tau^W_{h}\;.
    37		\end{equation}
    38		For each fixed $\tilde{u}$, the family $\{\tau^W_a(\tilde{u})\}_{a \in \F_q}$ is a projective measurement on $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$.
    39	\end{definition}

    41	\begin{definition}[Pulled-apart Pauli basis measurements]\label{def:tilde-m-measurement}
    42		\uses{def:s-w-marginals, def:tau-dot-product-projector, def:decoding-map}
    43		For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{M}$ define the measurement $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ by
    44		\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilde_M}
    45			\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a = \sum_{g} \hat{S}^W_g \ot \tau_{(\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a}^W(\tilde{u})\;,
    46		\end{equation}
    47		the sum ranging over $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$.     50	\begin{definition}[Pulled-apart Pauli observables]\label{def:tilde-w-observables}
    51		\uses{def:tilde-m-measurement, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:subfield-trace, def:generalized-pauli, lem:qld-4-7}
    52		Let $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ be the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ of Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}, and let $\tr = \tr_{q \to 2} \colon \F_q \to \F_2$ be the subfield trace.     53		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tildewj}
    54			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{a \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(e_j a)} \, \tilde{M}_a^{W,\tilde{u}}\;,
    55		\end{equation}
    56		acting on the same registers as $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$. Let $\tau^W(\cdot)$ denote the generalized Pauli $W$ observable (Definition~\ref{def:generalized-pauli}).     57		\begin{equation}\label{eq:tildewj-product-form}
    58			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})
    59			= \Big( \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\mathrm{Dec}(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \, \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z} \Big) \ot \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})\;,
    60		\end{equation}

    62		\[
    63			\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})\, \tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v}) =
    64			\begin{cases}
    65				\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})\, \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) & j \neq j'\;, \\
    66				(-1)^{\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_j \tilde{v}))}\, \tilde{Z}^{j}(\tilde{v})\, \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u}) & j = j'\;.
    67			\end{cases}
    68		\]
    69	\end{definition}

   106			\bigl( \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \bigl( \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}\;:

   148	\section{The swap unitaries and the extraction of the Pauli group}
   149	
   150	\begin{definition}[The swap unitaries]\label{def:v-swap-unitary}
   151		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, def:generalized-pauli, def:decoding-map, def:tilde-w-observables, def:tilde-m-measurement, def:indicator-vector}
   152		Define the linear map
   153		\[
   154			V_{\mathrm{A}} = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot \bigl(\tau^X(\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)) \, \tau^Z(\mathrm{Dec}(g_X))\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}''}\;,
   155		\]
   156		where $\tau^X(\cdot)$ and $\tau^Z(\cdot)$ are the generalized Pauli observables acting on $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$; note that the argument of $\tau^X$ is $\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)$ and the argument of $\tau^Z$ is $\mathrm{Dec}(g_X)$. Since the measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ is projective and the $\tau^X, \tau^Z$ observables are self-inverse,
   157		\[
   158			V_{\mathrm{A}} V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot \Id_{\mathrm{A}''} = \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''}\;,
   159		\]
   160		so $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ is a unitary acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$. The unitary $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ on $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$ is defined analogously. The conjugation action of these unitaries is exact. First, from the anti-commutation relation
   161		\[
   162			\tau^X(\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)) \, \tau^Z(\mathrm{Dec}(g_X)) \, \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\mathrm{Dec}(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \, \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \, \tau^X(\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)) \, \tau^Z(\mathrm{Dec}(g_X))
   163		\]
   164		and the product form \eqref{eq:tildewj-product-form} one computes, for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, and $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M$,
   165		\[
   166			V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot \bigl( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}''}
   167			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   168			V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \bigl( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;.
   169		\]
   170		Second, using the identities $\tau^X(s)\, \tau^Z_h \,\tau^X(s)^\dagger = \tau^Z_{h+s}$ and $\tau^Z(s)\, \tau^X_h\, \tau^Z(s)^\dagger = \tau^X_{h+s}$, the fact that $\F_q$ has characteristic $2$, and the linearity of the low-degree encoding $h \mapsto g_h$ \eqref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}, one computes, for all $u \in \F_q^m$ and $a \in \F_q$,
   171		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-unitary-6}
   172			V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   173			\qquad
   174			\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h \,:\, g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_h\;,
   175		\end{equation}
   176		and the same computation on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ gives the analogous identity for $V_{\mathrm{A}}$.
   177	\end{definition}
   178	
   179	\begin{lemma}[Extraction of the EPR state and the Pauli observables]\label{lem:qld-unitary}
   180		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, def:v-swap-unitary, def:expanded-state, def:projective-strategy-setup, def:generalized-pauli, def:EPR, def:povm-distance}
   181		There exists a function $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$, where $\delta_S$ is the function of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, and there exist unitaries $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ and $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ acting on registers $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, such that the following hold.
   182		\begin{enumerate}
   183			\item There exists a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ such that
   184			\[
   185				\bigl\| V_{\mathrm{A}} \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \bigr\|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}\;.
   186			\]
   187			\item For $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
   188			\begin{align*}
   189				V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \bigl(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}} \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''}\;, \\
   190				V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \bigl(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}} \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   191			\end{align*}
   192			where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''}$, with the answer summation over $h \in \F_q^{M}$ and no average over questions.
   193		\end{enumerate}
   194		The unitaries may be taken to be $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:v-swap-unitary}.
   195	\end{lemma}
   196	\begin{proof}
   197		\uses{def:v-swap-unitary, lem:qld-construct-the-paulis, lem:qld-win-implications, fact:triangle-for-simeq, def:bracket, lem:cancellation, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree, lem:qld-4-7}
   198		For the first item, the self-consistency of the observables $\tilde{W}^j$ (Item~2 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}) is equivalent to $\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M} \bra{\hat\psi} \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ot \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ket{\hat\psi} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2$; setting $\ket{\vartheta} = V_{\mathrm{A}} \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\hat\psi}$ and using the exact conjugation identities of Definition~\ref{def:v-swap-unitary}, this becomes $\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - \delta_S/2$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$, where $H_W = \E_j \E_{\tilde{u}} \, \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \ot \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = \bigl( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(s) \ot \tau^W(s) \bigr)^{\ot M}$ by the tensor factorization of $\tau^W(\tilde{u})$ and the invariance of the uniform average over $s$ under $s \mapsto e_j s$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}, $\E_{s,s'} \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \ot \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ on each pair of qudits, whence $H_X H_Z = \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$. The bounds $\| (\Id - H_W)\ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq \delta_S$ and $\bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 2\delta_S$, combined through the triangle inequality (see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}), give $\bra{\vartheta} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S}$; defining $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ as the normalization of $(\bra{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\vartheta}$, the overlap of $\ket{\vartheta}$ with $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$ is at least $\sqrt{1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S}} \geq 1 - O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$, which yields the first item with a bound of $O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$. For the second item, Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications} gives, on average over $u \in \F_q^m$, $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \Id \simeq_\eps \Id \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ and $\Id \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \simeq_\eps M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id$, where $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h : g_h(u) = a} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h$; combining these with Item~1 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} by Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle-for-simeq}, using $\delta_S \geq \eps$, yields $M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \Id \simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}} \Id \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a$. Writing $\ket{\Delta} = \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, the quantity to be bounded for the $\mathrm{A}$-side relation equals $2 - 2\sum_h \bra{\Delta} V_{\mathrm{A}} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \ot (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\Delta}$, since $(\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} = (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$. Replacing $(\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}$ by the averaged coarse-graining $\E_u \sum_{h' : g_{h'}(u) = g_h(u)} (\tau^W_{h'})_{\mathrm{B}''}$ costs at most $md/q$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree} (distinct $h \neq h'$ have distinct encodings $g_h \neq g_{h'}$, of total degree at most $md$), and by \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the resulting sum equals $\E_u \sum_{a} \bra{\Delta} V_{\mathrm{A}} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger \ket{\Delta}$. Exchanging $\ket{\Delta}$ for $\ket{\vartheta}$ costs $O(\delta_S^{1/4})$ by the first item, and the resulting expression $\E_u \sum_a \bra{\hat\psi} M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a]} \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \ket{\hat\psi}$ is at least $1 - O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$ by the $\simeq_{\sqrt{\delta_S}}$ relation above. Altogether the distance is $O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$; the $\mathrm{B}$-side relation is proved identically.
   199	\end{proof}

   201	\begin{remark}[A triangle-inequality step in the source argument]\label{rem:qld-unitary-triangle-slip}
   202		In the source proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary}, the triangle inequality gives $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \| \leq \| (\Id - H_X)\ket{\vartheta} \| + \| (\Id - H_Z)\ket{\vartheta} \| \leq 2\sqrt{\delta_S}$, so that $\| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \leq 4\delta_S$; the source instead asserts the bound $2\sqrt{\delta_S}$ for the \emph{squared} norm, which holds only when $\sqrt{\delta_S} \leq 1/2$, and carries the term $\sqrt{\delta_S}$ into the overlap bound $1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S}$. Either form of the bound yields an overlap of $1 - O(\sqrt{\delta_S})$ and leaves the final bound $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}} = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ unchanged asymptotically; a formalization should re-derive the intermediate constants.
   203	\end{remark}

   205	\section{Proof of the soundness of the Pauli basis test}
   206	
   207	We can now prove the soundness theorem for the Pauli basis test, stated as Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}.
   208	
   209	\begin{proof}
   210		\proves{thm:pauli}
   211		\uses{lem:qld-unitary, def:v-swap-unitary, thm:naimark, def:projective-strategy-setup, def:expanded-state, def:EPR}
   212		Let $(\ket{\psi},M)$ be a strategy for $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, where $\ket{\psi}$ is a bipartite state on registers $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$. By Naimark's theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark}, as formulated in~\cite[Theorem 5.1]{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}), at the cost of extending $\ket{\psi}$ by sufficiently many ancilla qubits initialized in the state $\ket{0}$, we may assume that the strategy is projective and that the state is padded as in the conventions of Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-setup}. Let $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ be the unitary acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ given by Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary}, and let $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}$ be the isometry mapping register $\mathrm{A}$ to registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$, where $\mathrm{A}'$ and $\mathrm{A}''$ are isomorphic to $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$, defined by
   213		\[
   214			\phi_{\mathrm{A}}\colon \ket{\theta}_{\mathrm{A}} \mapsto V_{\mathrm{A}} \bigl(\ket{\theta}_{\mathrm{A}} \ot (\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M})_{\mathrm{A}' \mathrm{A}''}\bigr)\;;
   215		\]
   216		define $\phi_{\mathrm{B}}$ analogously. Since the expanded state $\ket{\hat\psi}$ of Definition~\ref{def:expanded-state} is exactly $\ket{\psi}$ with the halves of $M$ pairs $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ appended locally in registers $\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ and $\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, we have $\phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} = V_{\mathrm{A}} \ot V_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\hat\psi}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-unitary} therefore yields a state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ such that
   217		\[
   218			\bigl\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \bigr\|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}
   219		\]
   220		and, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
   221		\[
   222			\phi_{\mathrm{A}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{A}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger \approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{A}''}
   223			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   224			\phi_{\mathrm{B}} \, (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_h)_{\mathrm{B}} \, \phi_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger \approx_{\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}} (\tau^W_h)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   225		\]
   226		where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$ and the answer summation is over $h \in \F_q^M$. This shows that the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ is a self-test, with robustness $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$, for the canonical Pauli strategy of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness}. Identifying the registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'$ with $\mathrm{A}'$ and $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$ with $\mathrm{B}'$ matches the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, in which $\phi_{\mathrm{A}}\colon \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}} \to \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}'} \ot \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{A}''}$. Finally, unpacking the dependence on the parameters $\eps, m, d, q$, the function $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ has the form $a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a > 1$ and $0 < b < 1$; see Remark~\ref{rem:pauli-robustness-form} for the reconciliation of this form with the statement of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}.
   227	\end{proof}
   228	
   229	\begin{remark}[Norm conventions in the robustness bound]\label{rem:pauli-robustness-form}
   230		The proof above, following the source, establishes the first conclusion of Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli} in the squared form $\| \phi_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \phi_{\mathrm{B}} \ket{\psi} - \ket{\mathrm{aux}} \ot \ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M} \|^2 \leq \delta_{\mathrm{qld}}$, whereas the theorem bounds the unsquared norm by $\delta_{\mathrm{qld}}(\eps,m,d,q)$.     84	\begin{definition}[Canonical complement]\label{def:canonical-complement}
    85		\uses{def:register-subspace}
    86		Let $\hat{E}$ be the standard basis of $V = \F^n$ and let
    87		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subset V$ be a set of $m$ linearly independent
    88		vectors. Write $v_i = \sum_{j=1}^n a_{i,j}\, \hat{e}_j$, and, using a
    89		canonical Gaussian-elimination algorithm valid over arbitrary fields,
    90		transform the $m \times n$ matrix $(a_{i,j})$ to reduced row echelon form
    91		$(b_{i,j})$. Let $J$ be the set of $m$ column indices containing the leading
    92		$1$ entry of each row of $(b_{i,j})$. The \emph{canonical complement of $F$}
    93		is the set of $n - m$ standard basis vectors
    94		\[
    95			F^\perp = \{\hat{e}_j : j \notin J\}\;.
    96		\]
    97		The canonical complement is a \emph{set} of vectors, not a subspace, and it
    98		depends on the set $F$ and not only on $\mathrm{span}(F)$. If $S$ is a
    99		register subspace spanned by $\hat{E}_0 \subseteq \hat{E}$, then the
   100		canonical complement of $\hat{E}_0$ is $\hat{E} \setminus \hat{E}_0$, and its
   101		span coincides with $S^\perp$.
   102	\end{definition}
   103	
   104	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:canonical-complement}
   105		\uses{def:canonical-complement, def:complementary}
   106		Let $S$ be the span of linearly independent vectors
   107		$F = \{v_1, \dots, v_m\} \subseteq V$, let $F^\perp$ be the canonical
   108		complement of $F$, and let $T = \mathrm{span}(F^\perp)$. Then
   109		\[
   110			S + T = V\;, \qquad S \cap T = \{0\}\;.
   111		\]
   112	\end{lemma}
   113	\begin{proof}
   114		\uses{def:canonical-complement}
   115		Let $A = (a_{i,j})$ be the $m \times n$ matrix whose rows are the $v_i$ and
   116		write $A = UB$ with $U$ invertible and $B$ in reduced row echelon form, so
   117		that the rows of $B$ are linearly independent and span $S$. The restrictions
   118		of the rows of $B$ to the columns in $J$ are still linearly independent and
   119		span $\F^m$, so for every $u \in V$ there is $v \in S$ that agrees with $u$
   120		on the coordinates in $J$. The difference $u - v$ is then supported on the
   121		coordinates outside $J$, that is, $u - v \in T$, which proves $S + T = V$.
   122		Counting dimensions forces $S \cap T = \{0\}$.
   123	\end{proof}

   303	\section{Polynomials and the low-degree code}
   304	% Paper label sec:ld-encoding kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   305	\label{sec:ld-encoding}
   306	
   307	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree]\label{def:polynomials-degree}
   308		\uses{def:polyfunc}
   309		An $m$-variate polynomial $f$ over $\F_q$ is a function of the form
   310		\[
   311			f(x_1, \dots, x_m) = \sum_{\alpha \in \{0, 1, \dots, q-1\}^m}
   312			c_\alpha\, x_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots x_m^{\alpha_m}
   313		\]
   314		with coefficients $c_\alpha \in \F_q$. It has \emph{individual degree (at
   315		most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$ only when $\alpha_i \le d$ for all
   316		$1 \le i \le m$, and \emph{total degree (at most) $d$} if $c_\alpha \neq 0$
   317		only when $\sum_i \alpha_i \le d$. (Affine) \emph{multilinear} polynomials
   318		are those of individual degree $1$. The set of $m$-variate polynomials of
   319		individual degree at most $d$, viewed as functions $\F_q^m \to \F_q$, is
   320		the set $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ of Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}.
   321	\end{definition}
   322	
   323	\begin{lemma}[Schwartz--Zippel lemma~\cite{Sch80,Zip79}]\label{lem:schwartz-zippel}
   324		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   325		Let $f, g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ be two unequal polynomials of total degree at
   326		most $d$. Then
   327		\[
   328			\Prb_{\bx \sim \F_q^m}[f(\bx) = g(\bx)] \le \frac{d}{q}\;.
   329		\]
   330	\end{lemma}
   331	\begin{proof}
   332		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   333		This is Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, stated and proved in
   334		Chapter~\ref{chap:preliminaries}; it is restated here under the label used
   335		by \cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   336	\end{proof}
   337	
   338	\begin{remark}\label{rem:schwartz-zippel-restated}
   339		The chapters on the classical low individual degree test already carry the
   340		Schwartz--Zippel lemma as Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree},
   341		together with its individual-degree consequence
   342		Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-individual}: distinct elements of
   343		$\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$ agree on at most an $md/q$ fraction of points. The
   344		Pauli basis test chapters invoke those nodes where the individual-degree
   345		form is needed; Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel} only preserves the label of
   346		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}.
   347	\end{remark}
   348	
   349	The Schwartz--Zippel lemma implies that low-degree polynomials form an
   350	error-correcting code with good distance, the \emph{low-degree code} (a special
   351	case of the generalized Reed--Muller code).
   352	
   353	\begin{definition}[Low-degree encoding]\label{def:low-degree-encoding}
   354		\uses{def:polynomials-degree}
   355		Fix an integer $m \in \N$ and let $M = 2^m$. For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$
   356		define the $m$-variate multilinear polynomial over $\F_q$
   357		\[
   358			\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)
   359			= \prod_{i : y_i = 1} x_i \cdot \prod_{i : y_i = 0} (1 - x_i)\;,
   360		\]
   361		identifying $\{0,1\}$ with a subset of $\F_q$. Restricted to the subcube
   362		$\{0,1\}^m$, the polynomial $\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}$ vanishes everywhere except
   363		at $x = y$, where it equals $1$. For $a \in \F_q^M$, label the coordinates
   364		of $a$ as $a_y$ for $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ (identifying $\{0,1\}^m$ with
   365		$\{1, \dots, M\}$ by the lexicographic ordering). The \emph{low-degree
   366		encoding of $a$} is the multilinear polynomial $g_a : \F_q^m \to \F_q$,
   367		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   368		\begin{equation}\label{eq:ld-encoding}
   369			g_a(x) = \sum_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} a_y \cdot \mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\;.
   370		\end{equation}
   371		For every $y \in \{0,1\}^m$ one has $g_a(y) = a_y$, and $g_a$ has total
   372		degree at most $m$.
   373	\end{definition}
   374	
   375	\begin{definition}[Indicator vector and linearity of the encoding]\label{def:indicator-vector}
   376		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:dot-product-orthogonal}
   377		For $x \in \F_q^m$, the \emph{indicator vector} is
   378		\[
   379			\mathrm{ind}_m(x)
   380			= \bigl(\mathrm{ind}_{m,y}(x)\bigr)_{y \in \{0,1\}^m} \in \F_q^M\;.
   381		\]
   382		With this notation the low-degree encoding satisfies, for every
   383		$a \in \F_q^M$ and $x \in \F_q^m$,
   384		% Paper equation label kept on the display it names.
   385		\begin{equation}\label{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}
   386			g_a(x) = a \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)\;;
   387		\end{equation}
   388		in particular the map $a \mapsto g_a$ is $\F_q$-linear.
   389	\end{definition}
   390	
   391	Since encodings $g_a$ are multilinear, hence of total degree at most $m$, two
   392	encodings of distinct strings agree on at most an $m/q$ fraction of points of
   393	$\F_q^m$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}.
   394	
   395	\begin{definition}[Decoding maps]\label{def:decoding-map}
   396		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding}
   397		For $H \subseteq \F_q$, the \emph{decoding map} $\mathrm{Dec}_H$ takes as
   398		input a polynomial $g : \F_q^m \to \F_q$ and returns the vector
   399		$a \in \F_q^M$ defined by: for all $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, set $a_y = g(y)$ if
   400		$g(y) \in H$, and $a_y = 0$ otherwise. For all $a \in H^M$ one has
   401		$\mathrm{Dec}_H(g_a) = a$. We write $\mathrm{Dec}(\cdot)$ for the boolean
   402		decoding map $\mathrm{Dec}_{\{0,1\}}(\cdot)$.
   403	\end{definition}

   411	\begin{definition}[Lines]\label{def:line}
   412		A \emph{line} $\ell$ in $\F_q^m$ specified by a pair
   413		$(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$ is the subset
   414		\begin{equation}\label{eq:line-set}
   415			\ell(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m\;.
   416		\end{equation}
   417		The vector $v$ is called a \emph{direction} of $\ell(u,v)$; the case $v = 0$
   418		is explicitly allowed, in which case the line is the singleton $\{u\}$. A
   419		line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate
   420		$i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ for which $v = e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   421		vector of $\F_q^m$; such a line is said to be \emph{parallel to the $i$-th
   422		direction}. A line $\ell(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists
   423		$i \in \{0, 1, \dots, m-1\}$ such that $v_1 = v_2 = \dots = v_i = 0$ (for
   424		$i = 0$ the condition is vacuous, so every line is diagonal).
   425	\end{definition}

    10	Throughout this chapter we work in the setting of
    11	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}: a projective strategy for the Pauli basis
    12	test game succeeds with probability at least $1-\eps$, and all operators act
    13	relative to the expanded state $\ket{\hat\psi}$ on registers
    14	$\mathsf{A}\,\mathsf{A}'\,\mathsf{A}''\,\mathsf{B}\,\mathsf{B}'\,\mathsf{B}''$
    15	(Definition~\ref{def:expanded-state}), where $n$ denotes the number of ancilla
    16	qudit registers, each isomorphic to $\C^q$, appended on each side. We write
    17	$q = 2^t$ (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $\tr:\F_q\to\F_2$ for the
    18	subfield trace. The points measurements
    19	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
    20	(Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}), their binary refinements
    21	\[
    22		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r}_b
    23		= \sum_{a \,:\, \tr(ar) = b} \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\,,
    24		\qquad r \in \F_q,\ b \in \F_2
    25	\]
    26	(Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-trace-projection}), and the lines
    27	measurements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},W),\ell}_{f}$
    28	(Definition~\ref{def:expanded-line-measurement}) are those constructed in
    29	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}, and $\delta_{\mathrm{acom}}(\eps)$ and
    30	$\delta_{\mathrm{Line}}(\eps)$ denote the error functions of
    31	Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons} and Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-line-cons},
    32	respectively.
    33	
    34	A subscript such as $(\,\cdot\,)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}$ indicates the pair of
    35	registers on which an operator acts; the two bipartitions in use are
    36	$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'$ versus $\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''$ and
    37	$\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ versus $\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$. The state-dependent
    38	distances $\approx_\delta$ (Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance}) and
    39	$\simeq_\delta$ (Definition~\ref{def:consistency}) are taken with respect to
    40	$\ket{\hat\psi}$ and averaged over the stated question distribution, and
    41	``all symmetric equivalents'' of an approximation is meant in the sense of
    42	Remark~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}. Between scalars, $\alpha
    43	\approx_\delta \beta$ means $|\alpha - \beta| \le O(\delta)$. For sums of
    44	measurement operators over outcomes satisfying a predicate we use the bracket
    45	notation of Definition~\ref{def:bracket}; for instance
    46	$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{[\mathrm{eval}_x(\cdot)=a,\ \mathrm{eval}_z(\cdot)=b]}
    47	= \sum_{f_X,f_Z \,:\, f_X(x)=a,\ f_Z(z)=b} T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}$.
    48	For a line $\ell$ (Definition~\ref{def:line}) and $k \in \N$ we write
    49	$\deg_k(\ell)$ for the set of polynomial functions on $\ell$ of degree at most
    50	$k$ in the line parameter, and
    51	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q) = \polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$
    52	(Definition~\ref{def:polyfunc}) for the $m$-variate polynomials over $\F_q$ of
    53	individual degree at most $d$; the restriction of an element of
    54	$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ to a line has total degree at most $md$.

    56	\section{Combined point measurements}
    57	
    58	The measurements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}$ and
    59	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}$ commute only approximately. The first goal of
    60	this chapter is to construct a single projective measurement that
    61	simultaneously measures both, first at points and then along lines. The
    62	construction of the combined point measurement proceeds in three steps: the
    63	binary refinements $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}$ and
    64	$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}$ are combined into a sandwich POVM, the
    65	resulting family is shown to satisfy an approximate linearity in the index
    66	pair $(r,s)$, and the following result of Natarajan and
    67	Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity} converts approximate linearity into exact
    68	linearity, from which a projective measurement with outcomes in $\F_q^2$ is
    69	assembled by Fourier averaging.
    70	
    71	\begin{theorem}[Quantum linearity test~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}]
    72		\label{thm:linearity}
    73		\uses{def:povm-distance}
    74		Let $0 \le \delta \le 1$, let $t$ be a positive integer, and let
    75		$\ket{\psi}$ be a state in a Hilbert space
    76		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}$. Let $\{\mathcal{O}^u\}$ be a
    77		set of observables indexed by $u \in \F_2^t$ acting on
    78		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}$, and suppose that on average over $u, u'$ chosen
    79		uniformly at random from $\F_2^t$ the approximate linearity
    80		\[
    81			(\mathcal{O}^u \, \mathcal{O}^{u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
    82			\approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^{u+u'})_{\mathsf{A}}
    83		\]
    84		holds with respect to $\ket{\psi}$. Then there exist an extended state
    85		$\ket{\psi'}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'\mathsf{B}}
    86		= \ket{\psi}_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}} \ot \ket{0}_{\mathsf{A}'}$
    87		in an extended space
    88		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{B}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ and
    89		observables $\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ acting on
    90		$\hilb_{\mathsf{A}} \ot \hilb_{\mathsf{A}'}$ such that for all
    91		$u, u' \in \F_2^t$,
    92		\[
    93			\mathcal{L}^u \, \mathcal{L}^{u'} = \mathcal{L}^{u+u'}
    94			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
    95			(\mathcal{L}^u)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
    96			\approx_\delta (\mathcal{O}^u)_{\mathsf{A}}\,,
    97		\]
    98		the latter with respect to $\ket{\psi'}$. Furthermore,
    99		$\mathcal{L}^u = \Id$ when $u = 0$.
   100	\end{theorem}
   101	\begin{proof}
   102		This is the quantum linearity test of Natarajan and
   103		Vidick~\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity}; no proof is given in
   104		\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}, which invokes the result directly. The statement is
   105		imported here as an external result; see
   106		Remark~\ref{rem:linearity-import}.
   107	\end{proof}
   108	
   109	\begin{remark}[Import status of the quantum linearity test]
   110		\label{rem:linearity-import}
   111		Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} is imported from
   112		\cite{Natarajan2017Linearity} and is not proved in the present
   113		development; its formalization is a separate work item. Two features of
   114		the statement are load-bearing for the proof of
   115		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}: the error is preserved exactly ($\delta$ in the
   116		hypothesis equals $\delta$ in the conclusion), and the linearity of the
   117		$\{\mathcal{L}^u\}$ is exact and holds for all pairs $(u,u')$, not merely
   118		on average.
   119	\end{remark}
   120	
   121	\begin{lemma}[Combined point measurements]
   122		\label{lem:qld-4-10}
   123		\uses{def:expanded-state, def:expanded-point-measurement,
   124			def:povm-distance, def:symmetric-equivalents}
   125		There exists a function $\delta_Q(\eps) = \poly(\eps)$ such that the
   126		following holds. For every $x, z \in \F_q^m$ and
   127		$\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there are
   128		projective measurements $\{\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}\}_{a,b \in \F_q}$ acting
   129		on $\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$ such that:
   130		\begin{enumerate}
   131			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random
   132			$x, z \in \F_q^m$,
   133			\begin{equation}
   134				\label{eq:qld-q-self-cons}
   135				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   136				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   137				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   138			\end{equation}
   139			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly
   140			random $x, z \in \F_q^m$,
   141			\begin{gather}
   142				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz}
   143				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   144				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   145				(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a} \,
   146				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   147				\\
   148				\label{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}
   149				(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   150				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   151				(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b} \,
   152				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   153			\end{gather}
   154		\end{enumerate}
   155		Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations also hold.
   156		The operators $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}$ and
   157		$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}$ do not commute in general, so the
   158		products in \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz} and
   159		\eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} differ and the two relations are separate
   160		conclusions.
   161	\end{lemma}
   162	\begin{proof}
   163		\uses{lem:qld-comm-cons, def:expanded-point-trace-projection,
   164			fact:add-a-proj, fact:agreement, lem:ortho, thm:linearity,
   165			lem:avg-closeness, lem:cancellation}
   166		Throughout the proof every intermediate error is a $\poly(\eps)$ function
   167		that may differ from one use of $\approx_\delta$ to the next. For
   168		$\omega = (x,z,r,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q$
   169		and $a, b \in \F_2$ define the sandwich POVM
   170		$\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b}
   171		= \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}_{b}
   172		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}_{a}
   173		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}_{b}$
   174		from the binary refinements of
   175		Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-trace-projection}; by the approximate
   176		commutation of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}, projectivity, and
   177		Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj}, on average over $\omega$ one has
   178		$\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b}
   179		\approx_{\sqrt{\delta_{\mathrm{acom}}}}
   180		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z,s}_{b}
   181		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x,r}_{a}$,
   182		and a Cauchy--Schwarz chain with successive errors
   183		$\delta_{\mathrm{acom}}^{1/4}$, $\delta_{\mathrm{acom}}^{1/4}$,
   184		$\sqrt{\eps}$, $\eps$ establishes the self-consistency
   185		$(\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \simeq_\delta
   186		(\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$, hence the
   187		corresponding $\approx_\delta$ relation by Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement}.
   188		The orthonormalization lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:ortho}) then produces
   189		projective measurements $\{\hat{L}^{\omega}_{a,b}\}$ with
   190		$\hat{L}^{\omega}_{a,b} \approx_\delta \hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b}$ on
   191		average over $\omega$. Next, the refined point measurements satisfy the
   192		exact linearity
   193		$\sum_{b+b'=c} \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r}_{b}
   194		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r'}_{b'}
   195		= \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u,r+r'}_{c}$
   196		(a direct consequence of projectivity of
   197		$\{\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\}$), which transfers, on average over
   198		$x, z, r, r', s, s'$, to an approximate linearity of the
   199		$\{\hat{R}^{\omega}_{a,b}\}$ in the index pair $(r,s)$ and then to the
   200		$\{\hat{L}^{\omega}_{a,b}\}$. Consequently the observables
   201		$\mathcal{O}^{\omega}
   202		= \sum_{a,b \in \F_2} (-1)^{a+b} \hat{L}^{\omega}_{a,b}$
   203		satisfy
   204		$\mathcal{O}^{x,z,r,s} \mathcal{O}^{x,z,r',s'}
   205		\approx_\delta \mathcal{O}^{x,z,r+r',s+s'}$
   206		on average; identifying $\F_q \cong \F_2^t$ so that the pair $(r,s)$
   207		ranges over $\F_2^{2t}$, Theorem~\ref{thm:linearity} applied for each
   208		fixed $(x,z)$ yields exactly linear observables
   209		$\{\mathcal{L}^{x,z,r,s}\}$ that are $\delta$-close to the
   210		$\{\mathcal{O}^{x,z,r,s}\}$ on average over $x, z, r, s$; no further
   211		extension of the state is needed because $\ket{\hat\psi}$ is padded with
   212		sufficiently many ancilla qubits in the zero state. Define
   213		$\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}
   214		= \E_{r,s} (-1)^{\tr(ra+sb)} \mathcal{L}^{x,z,r,s}$
   215		for $a, b \in \F_q$: exact linearity makes each $\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}$ a
   216		projection, and the family sums to the identity because
   217		$\mathcal{L}^{x,z,0,0} = \Id$, so $\{\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ is a
   218		projective measurement recovering $\F_q$-valued outcomes from the binary
   219		data by Fourier averaging over $(r,s)$. Its self-consistency
   220		\eqref{eq:qld-q-self-cons} follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:avg-closeness}
   221		together with the self-consistency of the $\{\mathcal{O}^{\omega}\}$;
   222		the consistency \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} follows from a Fourier
   223		computation that replaces $\mathcal{L}$ by $\mathcal{O}$, then by
   224		$\hat{R}$, then by the ordered product of refined point measurements, and
   225		finally resolves the averages over $r$ and $s$ using
   226		Lemma~\ref{lem:cancellation}; and \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-xz} follows
   227		by inserting one application of the approximate commutation of
   228		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons} into the same chain. Repeating the argument
   229		with the tensor factors on registers $\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'$ and
   230		$\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''$ gives all symmetric equivalents.
   231	\end{proof}

   233	\section{Combined line measurements}
   234	
   235	\begin{lemma}[Combined line measurements]
   236		\label{lem:qld-xz-lines}
   237		\uses{lem:qld-4-10, def:line, def:line-point-dist, def:consistency,
   238			def:bracket, def:expanded-state, def:symmetric-equivalents}
   239		There exists a function $\delta_P(\eps,m,d,q) = \poly(\eps, md/q)$ such
   240		that the following holds. For
   241		$\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ and every pair of
   242		lines $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ in $\F_q^m$ there exists a POVM
   243		$\{T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\}$ acting on $\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$,
   244		with answers consisting of pairs of polynomials
   245		$(f_X, f_Z) \in \deg_{md}(\ell_X) \times \deg_{md}(\ell_Z)$, such that on
   246		average over pairs $(\ell_X, x)$ and $(\ell_Z, z)$ independently sampled
   247		from the line-point distribution
   248		(Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist}),
   249		\[
   250			\big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}
   251			_{[\mathrm{eval}_x(\cdot)=a,\ \mathrm{eval}_z(\cdot)=b]}
   252			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   253			\simeq_{\delta_P}
   254			\big(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   255		\]
   256		as well as all symmetric equivalents of this approximation. Moreover, if
   257		$\ell_W$ is axis-parallel, then $f_W \in \deg_{d}(\ell_W)$.
   258	\end{lemma}

   260		\uses{def:expanded-line-measurement, lem:qld-4-10, fact:add-a-proj,
   261			lem:cool-closeness-fact, lem:qld-comm-line-cons, fact:agreement,
   262			fact:data-processing, lem:pasting, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}

   264		$(f_X, f_Z) \in \deg_{md}(\ell_X) \times \deg_{md}(\ell_Z)$, the sandwich
   265		operator
   266		$T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}
   267		= \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},X),\ell_X}_{f_X}
   268		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},Z),\ell_Z}_{f_Z}
   269		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},X),\ell_X}_{f_X}$,
   270		which forms a valid POVM; since the lines measurements come from a valid
   271		strategy for the low-degree test, on an axis-parallel line $\ell_W$ the
   272		outcome $f_W$ lies in $\deg_d(\ell_W)$, and this property is inherited by
   273		$T$. As intermediate consistency relations, applying
   274		Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj} to \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} and then
   275		Lemma~\ref{lem:cool-closeness-fact} gives, on average over uniform
   276		$x, z$,
   277		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   278		\approx_\delta
   279		\sum_b (\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   280		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$,
   281		and a direct norm computation from this display and
   282		\eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx} yields the marginal consistencies
   283		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_{\delta_Q}
   284		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$ and
   285		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{b})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \approx_{\delta_Q}
   286		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$.
   287		From items 1 and 3 of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-line-cons}, converting
   288		between $\approx$ and $\simeq$ with Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} and
   289		summing outcomes with Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing}, the lines
   290		measurements are consistent with the points measurements, and combining
   291		with the marginal consistencies gives, on average over the line-point
   292		distribution,
   293		$(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \simeq_{\delta_Q}
   294		(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},X),\ell_X}
   295		_{[\mathrm{eval}_x(\cdot)=a]})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}$
   296		together with the analogous relation for $Z$. The conclusion now follows
   297		from the pasting lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:pasting}) applied with
   298		$\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}$ in the role of the combined measurement,
   299		$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},X),\ell_X}$ and
   300		$\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Line},Z),\ell_Z}$ in the roles of the two factor
   301		measurements, $T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}$ in the role of the pasted measurement,
   302		$\delta := \delta_Q$, and $\eta := md/q$, the last justified by the
   303		Schwartz--Zippel bound (Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree})
   304		applied to the polynomials $f_X, f_Z$ of total degree at most $md$; the
   305		two hypotheses of the pasting lemma are supplied by the preceding display
   306		and by \eqref{eq:qld-q-self-cons}, and the distribution over
   307		$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is that of two independent uniformly random lines.

   309		error, a $\poly(\eps, md/q)$ function, and the identical argument with
   310		the registers modified gives all symmetric equivalents.
   311	\end{proof}

   313	\section{Applying the classical low-degree test}
   314	\label{sec:apply-ldt}
   315	
   316	The combined point and line measurements of the previous two sections are next
   317	merged into a single measurement returning a pair of global polynomials that
   318	encode the $X$-basis and the $Z$-basis information simultaneously. This is
   319	done by encoding the pair as one polynomial in $2m+2$ variables and invoking
   320	the quantum soundness of the classical low individual degree test
   321	(Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}).
   322	
   323	\begin{definition}[The combining map]
   324		\label{def:combine-map}
   325		\uses{def:polyfunc, def:line}
   326		For $f, g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$, the polynomial
   327		$\mathrm{combine}_{f,g} \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,2m+2}(\F_q)$ is defined by
   328		\[
   329			\mathrm{combine}_{f,g}(x, z, \alpha, \beta)
   330			= \alpha f(x) + \beta g(z)\,,
   331			\qquad x \in \F_q^m,\ z \in \F_q^m,\ \alpha \in \F_q,\
   332			\beta \in \F_q\,.
   333		\]
   334		The combining map is also defined for polynomials restricted to lines.
   335		Let $\ell$ be a line in $\F_q^{2m+2}$ with intercept
   336		$u = (u_X, u_Z, u_\alpha, u_\beta)$ and slope
   337		$v = (v_X, v_Z, v_\alpha, v_\beta)$, and let $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ be
   338		lines in $\F_q^m$ such that for every point
   339		$(x, z, \alpha, \beta) \in \ell$ it holds that $x \in \ell_X$ and
   340		$z \in \ell_Z$. Then for any two polynomials
   341		$f \in \deg_{md}(\ell_X)$ and $g \in \deg_{md}(\ell_Z)$, the polynomial
   342		$\mathrm{combine}_{f,g} \in \deg_{md+1}(\ell)$ is defined by
   343		\begin{equation}
   344			\label{eq:combine-lines}
   345			\mathrm{combine}_{f,g}(u + t \cdot v)
   346			= (u_\alpha + t \cdot v_\alpha)\, f(u_X + t \cdot v_X)
   347			+ (u_\beta + t \cdot v_\beta)\, g(u_Z + t \cdot v_Z)\,,
   348			\qquad t \in \F_q\,.
   349		\end{equation}
   350		The degree bound holds because $f$ and $g$, restricted to lines, are
   351		polynomials of degree at most $md$ in the line parameter, and each is
   352		multiplied by an affine factor of degree at most one.
   353	\end{definition}
   354	
   355	\begin{lemma}[Combined point measurement on the extended coordinates]
   356		\label{lem:qld-4-12}
   357		\uses{lem:qld-4-10, def:expanded-state, def:expanded-point-measurement,
   358			def:povm-distance, def:symmetric-equivalents}
   359		For all $x, z \in \F_q^m$, $\alpha, \beta \in \F_q$, and
   360		$\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there exists a
   361		projective measurement
   362		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c}\}_{c \in \F_q}$ acting on
   363		$\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$ such that the following holds, where
   364		$\delta_Q$ is the function of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}:
   365		\begin{enumerate}
   366			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) On average over uniformly random
   367			$(x, z, \alpha, \beta) \in \F_q^{2m+2}$,
   368			\begin{equation}
   369				\label{eq:qld-4-12-self-cons}
   370				(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   371				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   372				(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c})_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   373			\end{equation}
   374			\item (\textbf{Consistency with $\hat{M}$}) On average over uniformly
   375			random $(x, z, \alpha, \beta) \in \F_q^{2m+2}$,
   376			\begin{gather}
   377				\label{eq:qld-4-12-cons-m-hat}
   378				(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   379				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   380				\Big( \sum_{\substack{a,b:\\ \alpha a + \beta b = c}}
   381				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a} \,
   382				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}
   383				\Big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,, \\
   384				\label{eq:qld-4-12-cons-m-hat2}
   385				(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c})_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   386				\approx_{\delta_Q}
   387				\Big( \sum_{\substack{a,b:\\ \alpha a + \beta b = c}}
   388				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b} \,
   389				\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}
   390				\Big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,.
   391			\end{gather}
   392		\end{enumerate}
   393		Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations also hold.
   394	\end{lemma}
   395	\begin{proof}
   396		\uses{lem:qld-4-10, fact:data-processing}
   397		Define
   398		$\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{c}
   399		= \sum_{a,b \,:\, \alpha a + \beta b = c} \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}$,
   400		a coarse-graining of the projective measurement of
   401		Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}, hence itself projective. A uniformly random
   402		point of $\F_q^{2m+2}$ has uniformly random coordinates $(x,z)$, so the
   403		self-consistency and consistency properties follow from those of
   404		$\{\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}\}$ established in Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-10}
   405		together with Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing}, which shows that
   406		coarse-graining the outcomes preserves the $\delta_Q$ bounds.
   407	\end{proof}
   408	
   409	\begin{lemma}[Combined line measurement on the extended coordinates]
   410		\label{lem:qld-4-13}
   411		\uses{lem:qld-4-12, def:line, def:line-point-dist, def:consistency,
   412			def:bracket, def:expanded-state}
   413		There exists a function
   414		$\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}(\eps,m,d,q) = \poly(m^2\eps, md/q)$ such that
   415		the following holds. For every line $\ell$ in $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and
   416		$\hilb \in \{\hilb_{\mathsf{A}}, \hilb_{\mathsf{B}}\}$ there exists a
   417		POVM $\{\hat{Q}^{\ell}_{f}\}$ acting on $\hilb \ot (\C^q)^{\ot n}$ with
   418		outcomes $f \in \deg_{md+1}(\ell)$ such that on average over a uniformly
   419		random pair $(\ell, (x,z,\alpha,\beta))$ drawn from the line-point
   420		distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$,
   421		\begin{gather}
   422			\label{eq:qld-4-13}
   423			\big(\hat{Q}^{\ell}
   424			_{[\mathrm{eval}_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta)}(\cdot)=a]}
   425			\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'}
   426			\simeq_{\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}}
   427			\big(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}\,,
   428			\\
   429			\big(\hat{Q}^{\ell}
   430			_{[\mathrm{eval}_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta)}(\cdot)=a]}
   431			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{B}'}
   432			\simeq_{\delta_{\mathrm{combine}}}
   433			\big(\hat{Q}^{x,z,\alpha,\beta}_{a}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{B}''}\,,
   434			\notag
   435		\end{gather}
   436		where the answer summation is over $a \in \F_q$. Moreover, if $\ell$ is
   437		axis-parallel, then the outcome $f \in \deg_{d}(\ell)$.
   438	\end{lemma}
   439	
   440	Before proving the lemma we record definitions and estimates concerning
   441	distributions over lines and points. Recall from
   442	Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist} that the line-point distribution over
   443	$\F_q^m$ is an even mixture of an axis-parallel component $D_{\mathrm{ALine}}$
   444	and a diagonal component $D_{\mathrm{DLine}}$.

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in

    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99

   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}

   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.

   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}

1	\chapter{Strategy observables and the expanded space}
     2	\label{chap:qpbt-observables}
     3	% This chapter covers the first three subsections of the source appendix
     4	% ``Analysis of the Pauli basis test''
     5	% (references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex, lines 1-679).
     6	% The paper's subsection labels sec:qld-prelim, sec:commutation and
     7	% sec:expanding are kept on the sections below for cross-reference fidelity.
     8	% The source restates thm:pauli verbatim at the head of the appendix under the
     9	% label thm:pauli-appendix (lines 6-20); no duplicate node is created here,
    10	% and all references go to thm:pauli in Chapter chap:qpbt-test.
    11	
    12	This chapter and the two that follow contain the proof of the soundness
    13	theorem for the Pauli basis test, Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}, stated in
    14	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-test}. Starting from a strategy that succeeds in the
    15	game $G^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ with high probability, the proof
    16	constructs a representation of the Pauli group on the players' Hilbert space
    17	in several stages. In Section~\ref{sec:commutation} the strategy measurements
    18	are used to define a set of observables that correspond to a subset of the
    19	Pauli $X$ and $Z$ observables, and these observables are shown to
    20	approximately satisfy the associated Pauli group relations. In
    21	Section~\ref{sec:expanding}, ancillary registers containing EPR states are
    22	adjoined to the players' state, and a new set of approximately commuting
    23	observables acting on the expanded state is defined.
    24	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-combining} combines the approximately commuting
    25	observables into a strategy for the \emph{classical} low individual degree
    26	test and applies the soundness theorem of that test to construct a single
    27	projective measurement that simultaneously measures all of them.
    28	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-extraction} uses this simultaneous measurement to
    29	construct an exact representation of the Pauli group, shows that it is close
    30	to the original strategy observables on the expanded state, and deduces
    31	Theorem~\ref{thm:pauli}. Section~\ref{sec:qld-prelim} below collects
    32	preliminary definitions and lemmas used throughout the analysis.
    33	
    34	\section{Preliminaries}
    35	\label{sec:qld-prelim}
    36	
    37	\begin{definition}[Individual and total degree polynomial classes]
    38		\label{def:ideg-deg-polynomials}
    39		\uses{def:line}
    40		Given integers $d, m \geq 0$ and a prime power $q$, denote by
    41		$\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ the set of polynomials in $m$ variables over
    42		$\F_q$ with \emph{individual} degree at most $d$ in each variable. When
    43		the field is clear from context we write $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}$, and when
    44		the number of variables is also clear from context, $\mathrm{ideg}_d$. We
    45		denote by $\deg_d$ the set of polynomials with \emph{total} degree at
    46		most $d$.
    47		% The following usage is introduced only implicitly in the source, in the
    48		% statement of the lemma labelled lem:qld-comm-line-cons.
    49		For a line $\ell \subseteq \F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line}) we write
    50		$\deg_{md}(\ell)$ for the set of functions $\ell \to \F_q$ given by a
    51		univariate polynomial of degree at most $md$ in a parameterization of
    52		$\ell$.
    53	\end{definition}
    54	
    55	Throughout this chapter $q = 2^k$ with $k$ odd is an admissible field size
    56	(Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $n = 2^m$. Recall from
    57	Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} the low-degree code
    58	(see Definition~\ref{def:low-degree-encoding}), which maps each vector
    59	$h \in \F_q^{n}$, with
    60	coordinates indexed by binary strings of length $m$, to a polynomial
    61	$g_h \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ such that $g_h(u) = h_u$ for every
    62	$u \in \{0,1\}^m$; for $x \in \F_q^m$ the associated vector
    63	$\mathrm{ind}_m(x) \in \F_q^{n}$ satisfies
    64	$g_h(x) = h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(x)$ for all $h$. Recall also the finite
    65	field trace $\tr = \tr_{q \to 2} \colon \F_q \to \F_2$
    66	(see Definition~\ref{def:subfield-trace}).
    67	
    68	\begin{definition}[Commuting and anticommuting tuples]
    69		\label{def:anticommuting-tuple}
    70		% The quantity gamma is introduced in the source at eq:gamma-value, inside
    71		% the completeness analysis of the Pauli basis test; that label has no
    72		% corresponding node here, so the definition below is self-contained.
    73		\uses{def:low-degree-encoding, def:subfield-trace}
    74		For a tuple
    75		$\omega = (u_X, u_Z, r_X, r_Z) \in (\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$, let
    76		\[
    77			\gamma(\omega) \,=\, \tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)\,,
    78		\]
    79		where $r_W \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_W)$ is the scalar multiple of the
    80		vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_W) \in \F_q^{n}$, the middle $\cdot$ is the
    81		$\F_q$-inner product of two vectors in $\F_q^{n}$, and
    82		$\tr = \tr_{q \to 2}$. The tuple $\omega$ is called \emph{anticommuting}
    83		if $\gamma(\omega) \neq 0$, and \emph{commuting} if $\gamma(\omega) = 0$.
    84	\end{definition}
    85	
    86	The sign $(-1)^{\gamma(\omega)}$ is exactly the sign with which the
    87	generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X))$ and
    88	$\tau^Z(r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z))$ commute
    89	(see Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation});
    90	this is the source of the terminology.
    91	
    92	\begin{lemma}[Probability of anticommuting tuples]
    93		\label{fact:omega-anticomm-prob}
    94		% The source states this result in a `fact' environment; fact environments
    95		% become lemma nodes and the paper label is kept verbatim.
    96		\uses{def:anticommuting-tuple}
    97		The probability that a tuple $\omega = (u_X,u_Z,r_X,r_Z)$ sampled
    98		uniformly at random from $(\F_q^m)^2 \times (\F_q)^2$ is anticommuting is
    99		at least
   100		\[
   101			(1 - q^{-m}) \cdot (1 - q^{-1}) \cdot \Big(1 - \frac{md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}
   102			\,\geq\, \Big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\Big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}\,.
   103		\]
   104		The probability that $\omega$ is commuting is also at least
   105		$\big(1 - \frac{3md}{q}\big) \cdot \frac{1}{2}$.
   106	\end{lemma}
   107	\begin{proof}
   108		\uses{lem:schwartz-zippel, def:admissible-size, def:ideg-deg-polynomials, def:low-degree-encoding}
   109		The vector $\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)$ vanishes if and only if $u_X = 0$, and
   110		for all $r_X, r_Z, u_Z$,
   111		\[
   112			\tr\big( (r_X \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)) \cdot (r_Z \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u_Z)) \big)
   113			\,=\, \tr\big( (r_X r_Z) \cdot g_{\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)}(u_Z) \big)\,,
   114		\]
   115		where, for $u_X \neq 0$, the polynomial
   116		$g_{\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)} \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ is nonzero of
   117		total degree at most $md$. Condition on the event that $u_X \neq 0$,
   118		$r_X \neq 0$ and $g_{\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)}(u_Z) \neq 0$; by the
   119		Schwartz--Zippel lemma (Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel}) and the
   120		independence of $u_X, r_X, u_Z$, this event has probability at least
   121		$(1-q^{-m})(1-q^{-1})(1 - md/q)$. Conditioned on this event, the product
   122		$(r_X r_Z) \cdot g_{\mathrm{ind}_m(u_X)}(u_Z)$ is a uniformly random
   123		element of $\F_q$ over the choice of $r_Z$. Since $q$ is admissible, the
   124		trace of an element of $\F_q$ equals the coordinate sum of its binary
   125		representation (see Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}), so a uniform
   125		representation (see Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}), so a uniform
   126		element of $\F_q$ has trace $0$ with probability exactly $1/2$. Both
   127		bounds follow.
   128	\end{proof}
   129	
   130	\begin{definition}[Closeness of question-indexed operators]
   131		\label{def:approx-question-indexed-operators}
   132		\uses{def:povm-distance}
   133		Let $\{A^x\}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be families of operators (not necessarily
   134		POVM elements) indexed by questions $x \in \mathcal{X}$ but not by
   135		answers, let $\mu$ be a distribution over $\mathcal{X}$, and let
   136		$\ket{\psi}$ be a state, both fixed by context. Write
   137		$A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ to denote
   138		\[
   139			\E_{x \sim \mu} \bra{\psi} (A^x - B^x)^\dagger (A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi} \,\leq\, O(\delta)\,.
   140		\]
   141		This extends the answer-indexed closeness of
   142		Definition~\ref{def:povm-distance} to answer-free families of operators,
   143		such as observables; as there, the right-hand side allows a hidden
   144		universal constant.
   145	\end{definition}
   146	
   147	The following two lemmas relate the closeness between sets of operators and
   148	weighted sums of those operators.
   149	
   150	\begin{lemma}
   151		\label{lem:avg-closeness}
   152		\uses{def:approx-question-indexed-operators}
   153		Let $\{A^x\}$ and $\{B^x\}$ be operators indexed by a finite set
   154		$\mathcal{X}$, let $\mu$ be a probability distribution over
   155		$\mathcal{X}$, and let $\{\alpha_x\}$ be complex numbers with
   156		$|\alpha_x| \leq 1$. If $A^x \approx_\delta B^x$ on average over
   157		$x \sim \mu$, then $A \approx_\delta B$ for the single operators
   158		$A = \E_{x} \alpha_x A^x$ and $B = \E_{x} \alpha_x B^x$; that is,
   159		$\big\| (A - B) \ket{\psi} \big\|^2 \leq \delta$.
   160	\end{lemma}
   161	\begin{proof}
   162		Expand
   163		\[
   164			\Big\| \E_x \alpha_x (A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi} \Big\|^2
   165			\,\leq\, \Big( \E_x \big\| (A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi} \big\| \Big)^2
   166			\,\leq\, \E_x \big\| (A^x - B^x) \ket{\psi} \big\|^2
   167			\,\leq\, \delta\,,
   168		\]
   169		using the triangle inequality followed by Jensen's inequality.
   170	\end{proof}

   172	\begin{lemma}
   173		\label{lem:povm-to-obs}
   174		\uses{def:approx-question-indexed-operators, def:povm-distance}

   271			W^r(u) \,=\, \sum_{a \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(ar)} \, M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\,.

   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
